title: Dialogue on 2026 UNESCO GEM Report urges sustained action for learner participation and success
blurb: At the national launch of the 2026 Global Education Monitoring Report on access and equity in South Africa, the report director presented country findings. Between 2000 and 2024 the share of primary-age children out of school fell from 14% to 6%, and completion reached 97% in primary, 90% in lower secondary and 54% in upper secondary. Public spending on education stands at 6% of GDP, though pre-primary receives 0.1% of GDP. The report notes that no single reform will work and that resources should be directed towards disadvantaged regions, schools and learners.

title: UNESCO warns 95% upper-secondary completion may not be reached worldwide until 2105
blurb: UNESCO's 2026 Global Education Monitoring Report finds that, if current trends continue, the world may not reach 95% upper-secondary completion until 2105. Global completion rose between 2000 and 2024 from 77% to 88% at primary, 60% to 78% at lower secondary and 37% to 61% at upper secondary. An estimated 273 million children and young people were out of school in 2024, and the total has risen for seven consecutive years. In low-income countries, only 13 of the poorest young people complete upper secondary for every 100 of the richest. Education aid fell 8% between 2023 and 2024, and the report calls for policies suited to local conditions and barriers.

title: ‘Exam integrity’ faces scrutiny as parliamentary panel pushes for reforms
blurb: The Parliamentary Standing Committee on Education, Women, Children, Youth and Sports, reconstituted in September for a one-year term, has set its 2026-27 review agenda. Topics include national examination integrity and coaching centre regulation, NEP 2020 implementation, and the work of NCERT, CBSE and CABE, including CBSE affiliation and examinations. The panel will also look at student health, safety, mental well-being, inclusive education and grievance redressal, as well as AI in education. The previous committee had suggested computer-based tests, government-run exam centres and larger question banks.

title: Centre asks teacher trainees to teach 5-8 non-literate adults under new ULLAS guidelines
blurb: The Union Ministry of Education has released guidelines for teacher education institutions under ULLAS, the adult literacy programme, launched by Minister of State Jayant Chaudhary on October 28. Student teachers in NCTE-recognised programmes such as BEd and MEd will each help five to eight non-literate adults gain literacy and certification, with academic credits linked to learner certification. The framework assigns roles to NCTE, NCERT, SCERTs, DIETs and state literacy missions. ULLAS has a budget of ₹1,037.90 crore for 2022-23 to 2026-27, with around 4.03 crore learners registered as of September 2026.

title: Namibia Puts Unequal Education Opportunities in Focus at Global Report Launch
blurb: Namibia launched the 2026 Global Education Monitoring Report on access and equity at a national policy dialogue held in Windhoek on 30 September 2026. The report looks at equitable access through trends in early childhood education, out-of-school rates, completion rates and tertiary participation, and asks why some countries have expanded opportunities faster than others. The Deputy Minister said geography, poverty, disability and social background should never determine whether a learner gets an opportunity. Participants discussed how evidence-based planning, collaboration and fairer allocation of resources can improve participation and completion.

title: Cracks in Israel’s education system
blurb: Israel's results in the OECD's 2025 PISA assessment fell to their lowest level since the country began participating, with average scores of 433 in mathematics, 436 in reading and 442 in science, against OECD averages of 463, 461 and 482. Compared with 2022, maths fell by 25 points, reading by 38 and science by 23. A researcher at the Shoresh Institution says the war is not the only cause and points to a study finding that Israeli teachers have lower literacy, numeracy and problem-solving skills than peers in most OECD countries. He recommends changes to how teachers are recruited, trained and rewarded.

title: India's School Enrolment Reaches 24.72 Crore, Secondary Retention Stands At 51.9%
blurb: The UDISE+ 2025-26 report from the Ministry of Education records over 24.72 crore students in nearly 14.67 lakh schools, with an overall pupil-teacher ratio of 24:1 against the NEP 2020 benchmark of 30:1. Secondary-stage retention stands at 51.9%, compared with 98.5% at the foundational stage, while secondary dropout is 7%. Single-teacher schools fell by about 3% to 1,00,843, and zero-enrolment schools declined by 29% to 5,663. Computers are available in 69.9% of schools and internet in 67.4%, and girls make up 48.4% of enrolment.

title: CBSE Class 10 Exams 2027: Maths basic vs standard sample papers decoded, key questions and preparation tips
blurb: An analysis of the CBSE Class 10 Mathematics Basic and Standard sample papers for 2026-27 finds that both follow the same structure, and the board has confirmed there is no change in question paper design or assessment pattern. Each paper has 38 compulsory questions across five sections, carries 80 marks and runs for three hours. The long-answer and case-study sections together account for 32 marks, or 40% of the paper, so extended problem-solving carries weight. The Standard paper places more emphasis on application and reasoning, and the piece suggests practising every section and revising proofs.

title: Students win Viksit Bharat Buildathon for bomb-diffusing robot, smart glasses | India News
blurb: The Viksit Bharat Buildathon 2025, run by the Department of School Education and Literacy with Atal Innovation Mission and AICTE, named 10 national winners and entered the Guinness World Records as the largest innovation solution competition, with 287,967 project submissions. The winners shared ₹17.50 lakh, with five prototype-track teams receiving ₹2.5 lakh each and five idea-track teams ₹1 lakh each. Projects included a bomb-diffusing robot from Assam, affordable bone-conduction smart glasses from Uttar Pradesh and an urban air-purification concept from Gujarat. Selection ran through district, state and national tiers, recognising 1,000 district and 100 state awardees as well.

title: Even 95% secondary school completion may take until 2105 worldwide, warns Unesco
blurb: Coverage of UNESCO's 2026 Global Education Monitoring Report says that at current rates, 95% of young people would not complete upper-secondary education until 2105. Global completion rose between 2000 and 2024 from 77% to 88% at primary level, 60% to 78% at lower-secondary and 37% to 61% at upper-secondary. Late entry and grade repetition delay completion, with a nine percentage point gap between timely and eventual lower-secondary completion in low-income countries. Grade repetition has fallen by 62% in primary and 38% in lower-secondary since 2000.

title: Fix education to make AI work across Europe and Central Asia
blurb: This World Bank blog, drawing on the latest Economic Update for Europe and Central Asia, says the region needs stronger education to benefit from AI. PISA 2025 shows the regional average across maths, reading and science falling from about 421 points in 2018 to about 406, and in most countries at least half of 15-year-olds score below minimum proficiency. Students who check sources when using AI score far higher, yet only 29% in the region do so, against 45% in the EU. The author calls for stronger foundational skills, effective vocational education and lifelong learning.

title: Harnessing innovations in gender and learning to accelerate life outcomes
source: What Works Hub for Global Education
blurb: This What Works Hub for Global Education blog argues that learning programmes and gender-equality programmes should be designed together. Programmes on learning often overlook gender norms that shape whether children stay in school, while gender-focused efforts rarely measure literacy and numeracy. The authors cite evidence from coastal Kenya, where better literacy teaching raised reading outcomes and cut dropout, and from the LEAPS study in Pakistan, which found durable effects of quality primary schooling. They suggest joining the expertise of both sectors and point to co-investments that bring them together.

title: Jayant Chaudhary urges schools to join e-waste drive
blurb: Union Minister of State for Education Jayant Chaudhary called for school children to be involved in managing the growing challenge of e-waste, describing it as a shared responsibility of institutions, communities and citizens. He spoke at an event felicitating ten national-level winning teams of the Viksit Bharat Buildathon 2025, which received a Guinness World Records certification as the largest innovation solution competition. Organised by the Department of School Education with Atal Innovation Mission, NITI Aayog and AICTE, the initiative drew 2,87,967 project submissions from students, who were encouraged to identify problems and design solutions independently.

title: Parliamentary panel to examine integrity of national exams, need for reforms
blurb: The Parliamentary Standing Committee on Education, Women, Children, Youth and Sports has selected its subjects for 2026-27, including the integrity of national examinations, the need for public examination reforms and the functioning of coaching centres. It will also review progress on implementing NEP 2020 and the performance of NCERT, CBSE and the Central Advisory Board of Education. Student welfare in school education is on the agenda, covering health, safety, mental well-being, inclusive education and grievance redressal. The panel will further look at the impact of artificial intelligence and emerging technologies on education and students' employability, according to a Lok Sabha bulletin.

title: Jayant Chaudhary calls for collective action on e-waste management, involving school children
blurb: Minister of State for Education Jayant Chaudhary said at the felicitation of the national winners of Viksit Bharat Buildathon 2025 that growing e-waste is a challenge and that school children should be involved in its systematic management. He described it as a shared responsibility of institutions, communities and citizens. He stressed confidence, creativity and independent thinking among children and acknowledged teachers' mentoring role. The Buildathon is organised by the Department of School Education with Atal Innovation Mission, NITI Aayog and AICTE to encourage problem-solving, entrepreneurship and scientific curiosity among school students, and received a Guinness World Records certification.

title: Tools that fit: A guide for measuring family, school, and community engagement
blurb: Brookings has published a guide that helps education leaders measure family, school and community engagement. It walks users through three decisions: why they want to measure engagement, which approach best fits their questions and context, and which tools to use. The guide is accompanied by a workbook and an inventory of measurement tools for practitioners.

title: UDISE+ 2025-26: One in Three Indian Schools Still Has No Working Computer as AI Curriculum Rolls Out
blurb: An analysis of UDISE+ 2025-26 data finds that 5,41,851 of India's 14.67 lakh schools have no functional computer for teaching, even as the new Computational Thinking and AI curriculum for Classes 3 to 8 begins in 2026-27. The share of schools with a working teaching computer rose from 57.9% to 63.1% in a year, with private unaided schools at 74.0% against 59.4% for government schools. Bihar improved from 23.8% to 38.4%, while Meghalaya and West Bengal remain lowest. The authors suggest repairing the roughly one lakh non-working computers and giving teachers clear guidance on using AI safely.

title: Union Minister of State for Education Felicitates Winners of Viksit Bharat Buildathon 2025
blurb: Minister of State for Education Jayant Chaudhary felicitated the 10 national-level winning teams of Viksit Bharat Buildathon 2025 in New Delhi, where the event was certified by Guinness World Records as the largest innovation solution competition, with 2,87,967 project submissions. Organised by the Department of School Education and Literacy with Atal Innovation Mission, NITI Aayog and AICTE, it offered an award pool of over Rs 1 crore, including Rs 17.50 lakh for the national winners. The Minister also launched guidelines for Teacher Education Institutions under ULLAS, the adult literacy programme, and urged schools to involve children in e-waste management.

title: Sports and Education Ministries sign historic MoU with UNESCO to take clean sport values to every classroom
blurb: The Ministries of Education and of Youth Affairs and Sports exchanged an MoU with a United Nations agency to bring clean sport values into classrooms across India through a 'Sports Values in Every Classroom Toolkit'. Its video modules will be available in 13 Indian languages and aim to build respect, integrity and fairness in students. The MoU was exchanged at a Clean Sport Conclave held in Delhi. The Education Minister said it strengthens the link between education and sports, while the Sports Minister noted that over 350 awareness sessions reached 27,000 participants in 2025-26. Teachers are expected to bring the values to life in everyday school situations.

title: Lebanon Ministry of Education and Higher Education: The Impact of War on Lebanon's Education Sector
blurb: Lebanon's education ministry reports on how the war since March 2026 has affected its school system. About 20% of learners and 12% of teachers and other education staff were displaced, and roughly 27% of learners faced interruptions to their education. Of 1,089 facilities assessed in accessible areas, 436 reported being affected by attacks, including 64 severely damaged and 37 destroyed. The ministry adapted psychosocial and inclusive education services and delivered teaching onsite, online and in hybrid form. Recovery priorities include restoring learning continuity, rehabilitating safe facilities, supporting learner well-being and education personnel, and strengthening institutional preparedness.

title: CBSE unveils 6,000 sq ft experience centre in Delhi featuring 21 interactive exhibits
blurb: CBSE has opened a 6,000-square-foot Experience Centre at its integrated complex in Dwarka, New Delhi, with 21 interactive exhibits across 12 zones covering the history of education, science, career exploration and exam preparation. The Union Education Minister inaugurated it on October 27 and spoke of moving beyond rote learning towards experiential learning in line with NEP 2020. Career Explorer and Future of Professions exhibits support career guidance, and students use RFID smart cards to engage with displays. The minister also said 10,000 Atal Tinkering Labs are operational and 50,000 more will be established.

title: CBSE opens 6,000 sq ft experience centre in Delhi with 21 interactive exhibits
blurb: CBSE has opened a 6,000 sq ft experience centre at its headquarters in Dwarka, Delhi, with 21 interactive exhibits arranged across 12 zones. The zones cover the evolution of education, emerging technologies and career exploration. The exhibits are designed to promote experiential learning among students.

title: CBSE inaugurates experience centre in Delhi with 21 interactive exhibits
blurb: The CBSE Experience Centre has been inaugurated at the board's headquarters in Delhi, featuring 21 interactive exhibits designed to help students move beyond textbooks. Union Education Minister Pralhad Joshi opened the facility and said the centre reflects the objectives of the National Education Policy. He noted that the emphasis on marks has become so pervasive that parents and students often prioritise examination scores over genuine learning. The centre aims to give students a hands-on way to engage with concepts and to support learning that goes beyond marks.

title: Azim Premji Foundation CEO: How schools can help build a more humane world for everyone
blurb: The author argues that systems, including education, should not be designed only around self-interest and market logic. Taking school education as an example, he notes that over two decades evidence has shown private schools do not do better than public schools once children's economic backgrounds are accounted for. He says the case for privatisation overlooked information gaps, switching costs and the human tendency of teachers to care for children, alongside duty and professional pride. Drawing on research on animal behaviour and neuroscience, the piece suggests that institutions should build on this tendency towards goodness as much as on self-interest and rationality.

title: Ancient Nalanda, AI, interactive displays: Inside CBSE’s new Experience Centre | India News
blurb: The Union Education Minister inaugurated CBSE's Experience Centre at its New Delhi headquarters, a 6,000-square-foot space with 12 zones and 21 exhibits. It uses augmented and virtual reality, AI and holographic interactions to take students beyond textbooks, tracing India's educational heritage, scientific exploration and career discovery through exhibits such as Career Explorer. The Minister said the centre reflects NEP 2020's emphasis on experiential learning and urged recognising children's individual interests rather than judging them only by marks. The board's chairperson said that with AI now part of the curriculum, students need opportunities to engage with emerging technologies.

title: CBSE Experience Centre inaugurated in Delhi, features 21 exhibits across 12 zones
blurb: Union Education Minister Pralhad Joshi inaugurated the Central Board of Secondary Education Experience Centre at the CBSE Integrated Complex in Dwarka, New Delhi, on October 27, 2026. The centre is located at the board's headquarters and offers 21 exhibits spread across 12 zones. It is designed to give students an interactive learning environment that covers the evolution of education, emerging technologies and future career opportunities. The initiative adds a hands-on, experience-based space to the board's efforts to make learning more engaging for students.

title: Gabon Economic Update 2026: Investing in Education and Skills for More and Better Jobs and Inclusive Growth
blurb: The 2026 Gabon Economic Update reviews recent macroeconomic developments and gives special attention to education and skills for jobs. It proposes a dual strategy of restoring fiscal stability and improving the business climate while reforming education and skills. Unemployment affects around 17 percent of the working-age population and around 30 percent of youth, and the report notes learning and skills deficits. It recommends an education and technical and vocational training system that builds strong foundational, technical and job-relevant skills aligned with labour-market demand.

title: AI curriculum is being rolled out. But where are the working computers?
blurb: The analysis looks at school computer access as the new Computational Thinking and AI curriculum for Classes 3 to 8 begins in 2026-27. UDISE+ data show schools with a working computer for teaching rose from 57.9% to 63.1% in a year, and internet access from 63.5% to 67.4%, with notable gains in Bihar, Jharkhand and Uttar Pradesh. Still, 5,41,851 of 14.67 lakh schools lack a working computer, and 59.4% of government schools have one versus 74.0% of private unaided schools. The authors point to differences across states and the need for working devices alongside the curriculum.

title: We have become marksvaadis: Education minister flags marks obsession | India News
blurb: Union Education Minister Pralhad Joshi spoke at the launch of the CBSE Experience Centre at the board's New Delhi headquarters, encouraging a shift of focus from marks and rote learning towards students' self-confidence, curiosity and interests. The 6,000 sq ft centre has 12 zones and 21 exhibits on India's educational heritage, emerging technologies, career choices and environmental interconnectedness, with RFID smart cards for interactive use. CBSE chairperson Mandeep K Bhandari said the centre reflects the board's look beyond results towards overall development, and noted that Artificial Intelligence is now part of the curriculum.

title: Teacher pay in the US is relatively low and trending downward
blurb: Dan Goldhaber and Dick Startz examine teacher pay in the United States, which they describe as relatively low and trending downward. Their analysis looks at why teacher salaries are falling behind compared with other professions. They conclude that funding is not the obstacle to improving pay. The piece adds to the evidence on how compensation shapes the teaching workforce and offers a comparative reference point for countries thinking about teacher pay and school financing.

title: Pralhad Joshi calls for end to marks-driven education, seeks wider access to CBSE Experience Centre
blurb: Union Education Minister Pralhad Joshi spoke at the inauguration of the CBSE Experience Centre in Dwarka, New Delhi, and called for a shift from rote learning and a strong focus on marks towards experiential education, linking this to the aims of NEP 2020. He said the centre should be expanded, with ministry support, and made accessible to students from economically disadvantaged families. The 6,000 sq ft centre has 12 zones and 21 exhibits tracing the evolution of education, digital learning and career options, and uses RFID-enabled smart cards for interactive engagement with the exhibits.

title: Union Education Minister Shri Pralhad Joshi Inaugurates CBSE Experience Centre in New Delhi
blurb: Union Education Minister Pralhad Joshi inaugurated the CBSE Experience Centre at the CBSE Integrated Complex in Dwarka, New Delhi, an immersive space meant to take students beyond textbooks. The centre has 12 zones and 21 exhibits across 6,000 square feet, covering the history of Indian education, emerging technologies and career exploration through interactive displays and smart cards. The Minister called for moving away from rote learning and an excessive focus on exam scores, linking the initiative to the experiential learning goals of NEP 2020. He also noted that 10,000 Atal Tinkering Labs are operational and 50,000 more are planned.

title: CBSE Experience Centre traces evolution of India’s edu system from Gurukuls to digital classrooms
blurb: The CBSE Experience Centre, inaugurated by Union Education Minister Pralhad Joshi, houses 12 zones and 21 exhibits across 6,000 square feet, offering a technology-led look at India's educational heritage, science and careers. Visitors begin with a short film, Shiksha Ki Kahani, tracing education from the Gurukul system and Nalanda to digital classrooms, and see CBSE archival records dating to 1935. An exam-focused kiosk uses games based on the Prime Minister's Pariksha Pe Charcha mantras, while career exhibits such as Career Explorer and Future of Professions show how work may change. Holograms of figures including BR Ambedkar and APJ Abdul Kalam feature as well.

title: When AI can teach, what is the teacher for? | Hindustan Times
blurb: The author argues that AI will take over much explaining, drilling and correcting, so schools must redesign around the teacher's role rather than simply add AI to the existing model. He cites a survey in which 35% of children using educational technology already use generative AI. He recommends assessment that tests reasoning rather than answers, project-based learning on real local problems, and AI literacy built into teacher education and ongoing professional development. He adds that AI can help personalisation but could widen gaps if tools reach under-resourced schools without trained teachers.

title: Education has become ‘marks-wadi’, rote learning must go: Pralhad Joshi
blurb: Speaking at the launch of the CBSE Experience Centre, Union Education Minister Pralhad Joshi called for replacing rote learning with experiential learning. He said the system, and many parents with it, has become overly focused on marks, with much of a student's time going into memorising and working out how to score. The Minister said hands-on learning can build confidence and help make students job-ready. He described the centre as an initiative that supports this shift towards practical, student-centred education in line with the National Education Policy.

title: Can India’s education system do more to counter child marriage? | Hindustan Times
blurb: The author argues that the education system can do more to prevent child marriage, alongside laws and awareness campaigns, because girls who stay in school are less likely to marry before 18. He says enrolment alone is not enough, since household duties, cost, safety and distance to secondary school can keep girls out, and he suggests teachers can act as early-warning points through training and referral systems. He recommends career counselling, vocational and life-skills exposure, engaging boys, parents and communities, and data-led approaches for states with higher prevalence. He adds that education works best together with law enforcement and social protection.

title: Only 59 girls complete upper secondary education for every 100 boys in rural India: UNESCO report
blurb: UNESCO's 2026 Global Education Monitoring Gender Report finds that 59 girls complete upper secondary education for every 100 boys in rural India, while urban India has reached parity. The report uses the World Inequality Database on Education to show how location and household wealth shape outcomes behind national averages. Globally, gender parity in enrolment has been achieved from pre-primary to upper secondary, but completion remains uneven, and the broader 2026 GEM Report estimates 273 million children and young people were out of school in 2024. It identifies child marriage, early pregnancy and limited support for returning students as key barriers.

title: JEE Advanced students seek third attempt, raise concerns over CBSE attendance rule
blurb: A petition signed by nearly 12,700 students asks the Joint Admission Board, the IIT Council and the Ministry of Education to review the JEE Advanced limit of two attempts. The students say the 75 per cent attendance requirement for CBSE Class 10 and 12 board examinations leaves regular schoolgoers with limited time for entrance preparation. They also point out that JEE Main allows more attempts than JEE Advanced. The IIT Kanpur Director has said a possible third attempt is under discussion, though no decision has been taken and the current eligibility rules remain unchanged.

title: How COP31 could shift climate education from awareness to action
blurb: The article says the COP31 climate summit in Antalya could give climate change education a more measurable policy focus. Countries are expected to discuss integrating climate topics into curricula, training teachers and supporting community learning. The author argues that India is well placed to showcase its own approach to climate education at the summit.

title: CBSE hosts national summit on school-to-work transition, digital skills and career guidance
blurb: CBSE is holding its fourth National Summit on facilitating the school-to-work transition in New Delhi on October 26 and 27, with the Sahodaya School Complexes of Delhi-NCR. The Secretary of the Department of School Education and Literacy named four priorities: technology and digital safety, creativity and innovation, recognition of skills through the National Credit Framework, and career guidance with equitable pathways. He encouraged closer links between school, higher education, skilling and employment, in line with NEP 2020. Teachers from affiliated schools are presenting papers and posters on skill education practices, assessment and digital integration.

title: CBSE Open-Book Exams: How Students May Need To Change Their Study Strategy
blurb: A national media piece looks at open-book examinations under CBSE and what the format could mean for how students prepare. It discusses how study habits may shift from recall towards understanding, application and analysis of concepts. The article offers students practical pointers on adjusting their preparation strategy to suit this style of assessment.

title: CBSE to inaugurate experience centre in Dwarka today; facility to showcase board’s initiatives and innova
blurb: The Central Board of Secondary Education is scheduled to inaugurate an Experience Centre on October 27, 2026, at its Integrated Office Complex in Dwarka, New Delhi. The centre is designed as an interactive space where visitors can explore the board's initiatives and innovations in school education.

title: CBSE National Summit on School-to-Work Transition Begins; Explores New Approaches to Skill Education
blurb: The Central Board of Secondary Education has begun a national summit on the school-to-work transition. The summit explores new approaches to skill education in schools.

title: CBSE National Summit 2026: Focus on school-to-work transition, digital skills and career guidance
blurb: The Central Board of Secondary Education is holding its fourth National Summit on facilitating the school-to-work transition in New Delhi on October 26 and 27, 2026. It is organised with the Sahodaya School Complexes of Delhi/NCR. The summit brings together school leaders, educators, industry experts and policymakers to discuss how to prepare students for changing workforce requirements and future careers. Reported focus areas include digital skills and career guidance.

title: Teaching above students' level: educational barrier to progress
blurb: This evidence summary examines why teaching to a grade-level curriculum can leave children behind when they are well below it. It cites randomized evaluations of Teaching at the Right Level, with language gains of 0.15 standard deviations in Haryana and 0.70 in Uttar Pradesh, and a Ghana trial showing gains of about 0.1 despite implementation problems. It notes that results depended on ongoing mentorship and on grouping children by learning level during the school day, not on teacher training or materials alone. ASER 2024 data show 23.4% of Grade 3 government school children could read a Grade 2 text.

title: The promises and perils of multipolarity in education aid
blurb: A think piece argues that international education aid is moving from a system led by a few institutions such as the World Bank, UNICEF and the UN towards a multipolar landscape. Donor fatigue and shifting politics in traditional donor countries are reducing funding, while China, regional development banks, Gulf states and private philanthropies give countries a wider choice of partners. The author says this gives governments in the Global South more agency to negotiate terms and align aid with domestic needs. It also cautions that uncoordinated bilateral deals could leave education systems with fragmented policies, misaligned curricula and inconsistent teacher training.

title: Dr. Amy Jo Dowd’s Guest Curation
blurb: A guest curation from EdTech Hub's Signal Library by Dr Amy Jo Dowd of Brink Foundation looks at how gender bias can be carried into AI in education. The three selected resources show AI tools mirroring bias, for example in recommendation letters and role suggestions, and describe a digital gender divide covering access, use and empowerment, including cyberviolence against minors. A third piece uses global data to show girls' early schooling advantage reversing by the end of secondary school and in adult outcomes. The curator concludes that expanding access to education and technology is not enough unless the norms and biases within systems are also addressed.

title: IIT Mandi launches ‘Science on Wheels’ to bring hands-on science education to schools across HP
blurb: The Science on Wheels programme, backed by the Department of Science and Technology, has been extended to Himachal Pradesh by IIT Mandi together with Plaksha University and the Igniting Dreams of Young Minds Foundation. The state segment was launched on October 17 at the IIT Mandi Campus School and aims to cover 50 schools, beginning with government senior secondary schools in Mandi district. The programme has already reached more than 7,500 students across 70 schools in Chhattisgarh and Punjab. For students in Classes VI to XII, particularly in rural areas, it offers about six hours of hands-on learning per school on space technology, robotics, sustainability and water filtration.

title: Promotion of Mother Tongue-based Education
blurb: This Press Information Bureau release on promotion of mother tongue-based education begins from Article 350A of the Constitution, which says that every State and local authority should endeavour to provide adequate facilities for instruction in the mother tongue at the primary stage of education for children of linguistic minority groups. The constitutional provision frames the Centre's approach to multilingual and mother-tongue instruction in the early years of schooling.

title: CBSE Organises 4th National Summit on Facilitating School-to-Work Transition in New Delhi
blurb: CBSE, together with the Sahodaya School Complexes of Delhi/NCR, is holding its 4th National Summit on facilitating school-to-work transition in New Delhi on October 26-27. School Education Secretary T. K. Anil Kumar set out four priorities: technology, digital safety and skills; design, creativity and innovation; recognition of skills across education systems through the National Credit Framework; and career guidance with equitable pathways. The summit brings together school leaders, educators, industry experts and policymakers, and educators from CBSE-affiliated schools are presenting case papers and posters on skill education practices, in line with NEP 2020.

title: NCERT Minority Cell reviews school access, dropout rates and teacher training at first meeting of 2026-27
blurb: The National Council of Educational Research and Training held the first meeting of its Minority Cell for the 2026-27 session on October 23 at the North East Regional Institute of Education in Umiam, Meghalaya. The meeting reviewed school access, dropout rates and teacher training as they relate to minority communities. The Cell recommended strengthening teacher training and undertaking region-specific research to better understand and address the educational needs of different areas.

title: UN report flags child marriage as a barrier to girls’ education, highlights India’s rural gender gap
blurb: Girls' access to education has improved, but child marriage, early pregnancy and a lack of support for young mothers still keep many from finishing school, the 2026 Global Education Monitoring Gender Report finds. In rural India only 59 girls complete upper secondary education for every 100 boys, while urban areas have reached parity. Globally the share of girls married before 18 fell from 25 per cent in 2000 to 18 per cent in 2025, while in sub-Saharan Africa an estimated 6 million pregnant girls and young mothers were out of school in 2024. Only 35 per cent of countries explicitly protect the right of pregnant and parenting girls to education.

title: CBSE is organising the 4th National Summit on ‘Facilitating School-to-Work Transition’ in New Delhi
blurb: The Ministry of Education announced that a two-day national summit on facilitating the school-to-work transition is under way in New Delhi on October 26 to 27, 2026, organised together with the Sahodaya School Complexes of Delhi/NCR. The Secretary of the Department of School Education and Literacy outlined four priorities: technology, digital safety and skills; design, creativity and innovation; recognition of skills through the National Credit Framework; and career guidance with equitable pathways. School leaders, educators, industry experts and policymakers are discussing future workforce needs and ways to link skill education with mainstream schooling, in line with NEP 2020.

title: Schools still failing girls on periods: SC seeks answers on menstrual hygiene
blurb: The Supreme Court has asked states and Union Territories to report on how they are implementing its January 30, 2026 judgment on menstrual hygiene in schools, noting that most had not responded to the Centre's requests for information. Defaulting governments have four weeks to file detailed affidavits, with chief secretaries facing possible contempt notices, and the next hearing is on December 14, 2026. The judgment requires free sanitary products, separate functional toilets with water and soap, safe disposal systems, menstrual health education and trained teachers in all schools. It also directs a move towards biodegradable, compostable sanitary napkins.

title: NCERT’s AI module for Classes 9-12 teaches students to spot deepfakes, check facts and protect data
blurb: The National Council of Educational Research and Training has released a 20-hour module on computational thinking and artificial intelligence for Classes 9 to 12, developed with faculty from IIT Madras and IIT Jodhpur. It needs no prior AI knowledge and uses activity-based learning that can be done with or without digital devices. Its five units cover how AI works and where it fails, how machines learn from examples, spotting deepfakes and misinformation using five verification checks, data privacy and consent, and using AI tools responsibly without replacing independent thinking.

title: Hands-On Learning: How NCERT’s AI module uses real-life examples, classroom activities to teach Classes 9 to 12 | India News
blurb: NCERT has released a 20-hour introductory module on computational thinking and AI for Classes 9 to 12, developed with faculty from IIT Madras and IIT Jodhpur. It assumes no prior knowledge and uses activity-based learning across five units, from spotting AI in daily life and training a simple classifier to checking AI errors, protecting personal data and using AI tools responsibly. Activities can be done with or without digital devices, so schools with limited access can take part. Students record their work in a portfolio called the Curious Notebook, which includes an AI diary, a verification checklist and a prompt library.

title: At COP, a move from climate learning to climate action
blurb: This opinion piece by a TERI director argues that climate change education should move from awareness to competency-based learning, and that the COP31 summit starting on November 9 is a chance to commit to measurable national goals. It traces India's journey from the 1991 Supreme Court direction on environmental literacy to NEP 2020 and NCF-SE 2023, and notes the global Greening Education Partnership. The author says teacher capacity-building and regional knowledge platforms need more attention. India can showcase Eco Clubs, Mission LiFE and NISHTHA, and stress climate literacy, resilience and green skills.

title: CBSE makes AI a part of formal teaching, NCERT develops module
blurb: CBSE is moving artificial intelligence from an optional subject towards a basic skill for its students, with more formal teaching in schools. NCERT has developed a 20-hour introductory AI module for Classes IX to XII. The module has been earmarked for school-based assessment. It covers practical skills such as spotting deepfakes and questioning a chatbot's confident but incorrect answers.

title: Schools collect 4.27 lakh e-waste items under Ministry of Education campaign
blurb: Schools across India collected 4.27 lakh discarded electronic items in a nationwide e-waste campaign held under the Ministry of Education's Eco Clubs for Mission LiFE initiative. A total of 57,271 schools took part, involving about 33 lakh people including 30.22 lakh students and 2.78 lakh teachers, and 39,494 collection corners were set up in schools. Webinars and guidance for teachers covered safe handling, repair, reuse, recycling and data protection, and standard operating procedures, an e-book and regional-language material were prepared. Organisers said the work will continue through school sustainability activities and better records of collection and handover.

title: The UN at 81: Education for all remains an unfinished promise
blurb: The author reflects on the United Nations at 81 and argues that education for all remains an unfinished promise. Enrolment rose by 327 million students between 2000 and 2024 to 1.4 billion, yet an estimated 273 million children and young people were out of school in 2024, a figure that has risen for seven consecutive years. The piece notes that UN resolutions are not enforceable and depend on national budgets, and that one in four countries meets neither spending benchmark. It points to India's public spending of about 4.12 per cent of GDP in 2021-22 against the 6 per cent set in NEP 2020.

title: Chartbook 480 France’s schools system may be bad, but we should all be protesting the decline in education!
blurb: An analysis of PISA 2025 results asks how weak French schooling really is, as student protests unfold in France. It finds French median reading performance well below the average of rich-country peers, with the bottom tenth ranking seventh from the bottom of 24 systems and top performers scoring lower than expected. The share of 15-year-olds who are barely literate or out of school rose from 28.6 percent in 2015 to 40.8 percent in 2025, while top performers fell from 11.4 to 4 percent, mostly since 2022. The author notes that similar post-pandemic declines, especially in mathematics, appear across wealthy countries.

title: United Nations' Report Flags Early Marriage As Major Barrier To Girls' Education Worldwide
blurb: A United Nations report identifies early marriage as a major barrier to girls' education worldwide. The coverage highlights how marrying young limits the number of years girls spend in school and their wider opportunities, and points to the importance of keeping girls learning as a way to support their long-term wellbeing.

title: Ethical boundaries to detecting deepfakes: NCERT introduces 20-hour AI module for classes 9-12
blurb: NCERT has released a 20-hour introductory module on computational thinking and artificial intelligence for Classes 9 to 12, developed in consultation with IIT Madras and IIT Jodhpur. The activity-based module is designed for students with no prior knowledge of AI and covers how machines learn from examples, everyday AI applications, deepfake detection and data privacy. Activities can be done with or without digital devices, so schools with different resources can use it. It stresses ethical and safe use, including misinformation, fairness and checking AI outputs, while keeping human judgement central.

title: NCERT introduces 20-hour AI module for classes 9-12, covers deepfakes and data privacy
blurb: A new 20-hour, activity-based module on computational thinking and artificial intelligence has been introduced for Classes 9 to 12, aligned with NEP 2020 and developed with experts from two technical institutes. Its five units cover everyday uses of AI, training simple image classifiers, misinformation, deepfakes and AI hallucinations, data privacy and consent, and writing and refining prompts. Teacher guidance suggests schools can use devices, teacher-led demonstrations or offline paper-based discussions, so schools with limited connectivity can take part. The module encourages students to treat AI as an aid to independent thinking and to keep a notebook of reflections.

title: Qatar students record decade-high science results as AI adoption grows
blurb: Results from the 2025 round of an international assessment of 15-year-olds show Qatar's science, mathematics and reading scores among the highest it has recorded, with science averaging 434 points. The share of students below baseline proficiency in science fell by seven percentage points between 2015 and 2025. About 46 percent of students reported using AI chatbots for learning at least weekly, in line with the average across participating countries. Around 34 percent used them for preliminary research or to summarise reading, and 30 percent to draft text. The sample covered 6,674 students in 246 schools.

title: NCERT introduces 20-hour AI module for Classes 9-12, covers deepfakes, data privacy | India News
blurb: NCERT has released an activity-based, 20-hour introductory module on computational thinking and artificial intelligence for Classes 9 to 12, aligned with NEP 2020 and designed for students with no prior knowledge of AI. It has five units covering AI in everyday life, how machines learn, why AI gets things wrong, data privacy and responsible use, and modern AI tools. Students practise verifying information, spotting deepfakes and misinformation, and learn about India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, while keeping a Curious Notebook of reflections. The module favours practical exercises and discussion over memorisation and aims to build informed, responsible users of technology.

title: Teacher Safety and Professional Authority in India’s Schools
blurb: The piece examines calls from school management associations for a dedicated law protecting teachers and schools from violence, citing incidents reported in several parts of the country. It notes that no centralised data exists on attacks against teachers, so the scale of the issue and any differences between government and private schools cannot yet be compared. The author argues that teachers need protection and professional authority, balanced by accountability, including clear limits on corporal punishment and humiliation. It suggests evidence-led reform, with fair channels for parents and students to raise genuine complaints.

title: NCERT introduces AI, computational thinking module for Classes 9-12; here's what it covers
blurb: The National Council of Educational Research and Training has developed an introductory module on artificial intelligence and computational thinking for students in Classes 9 to 12. Aligned with NEP 2020 and designed for learners with no prior AI knowledge, it uses activity-based exercises and discussions that can be run with or without digital devices. Students are introduced to data privacy, misinformation, fairness and digital safety, and are encouraged to verify AI-generated information and keep human judgement central. A timeline for classroom implementation has not yet been specified.

title: NCERT Introduces Module On Computational Thinking, Artificial Intelligence For Classes 9-12
blurb: NCERT has developed an introductory module on Computational Thinking and Artificial Intelligence for students in Classes 9 to 12. It aims to build critical thinking, creativity and systematic problem-solving through classroom discussions, practical exercises, experiments and self-reflection. Teachers can deliver the lessons with or without digital tools, so schools with varied infrastructure can adopt it. The module covers digital safety, data privacy, fairness and online security, and encourages students to judge the reliability of AI-generated content. It is aligned with the priorities of NEP 2020.

title: NCERT releases AI module for Classes 9 to 12; deepfakes, ethical usage in focus | India News
blurb: NCERT has released an activity-based, 20-hour introductory module on computational thinking and artificial intelligence for Classes 9 to 12, developed with faculty from IIT Madras, IIT Jodhpur and NCERT. It is aligned with NEP 2020 and designed for students with no prior knowledge of AI. The five units cover AI in everyday life, how machines learn, why AI gets things wrong, data privacy and responsible use, and working with modern AI tools. Activities can be done with devices, on a shared screen or in unplugged form, so schools with limited connectivity can take part.

title: NCERT’s new AI module for Classes 9-12 targets misinformation and data privacy
blurb: NCERT has brought out a new module on artificial intelligence for students in Classes 9 to 12. It is designed for learners with no prior knowledge of AI and encourages critical thinking, creativity, problem-solving and the responsible use of emerging technologies. The module takes an experiential, activity-based approach, using discussions, practical exercises, experimentation and reflection. Its content addresses issues such as misinformation and data privacy, helping students engage with AI tools thoughtfully and safely.

title: Where curiosity gets to build: Inside the AI Olympiad, in photos and students’ own words
blurb: Experts at the launch of the GLF AI Olympiad 2026 discussed why AI education should begin early, so that children are prepared for an AI-driven world. They also spoke about how early exposure can help bridge learning gaps. The piece presents the event through photographs and students' own words about building and learning with AI.

title: NCERT introduces Computational Thinking and AI module for Classes 9 to 12
blurb: NCERT has introduced a module on Computational Thinking and Artificial Intelligence for students in Classes 9 to 12, prepared under the aegis of the Ministry of Education. It needs no prior subject knowledge and uses activity-based learning such as discussions, experiments and self-reflection, which can be done with or without digital tools. Computational thinking is presented as a systematic way to solve problems, and a key section covers safe and responsible AI use, including data privacy, misinformation, fairness and verifying AI-generated content. The module supports the National Education Policy 2020 focus on 21st-century skills.

title: NCERT launches AI, computational thinking module for Grades 9-12
blurb: NCERT has introduced an introductory module on Computational Thinking and Artificial Intelligence for students in Grades 9 to 12, aligned with the National Education Policy 2020. The beginner-friendly module uses hands-on, activity-based learning that can be done with or without digital devices, and builds critical thinking, creativity and problem-solving. It gives particular emphasis to the ethical and safe use of AI, including data privacy, misinformation, fairness, digital safety and verifying AI-generated information, and uses Aadhaar and UPI as examples of AI in India. Students are also taught to protect personal information and seek help from trusted adults.

title: Green shoots in global learning: lessons from the Philippines, Cambodia and Zambia’s PISA results
source: What Works Hub for Global Education
blurb: An evidence blog from the What Works Hub for Global Education examines the latest PISA results for the Philippines, Cambodia and Zambia, which improved while many countries saw stagnation or decline. Compared with the 2017/18 baselines, all three made notable gains over a relatively short period, though they remain below the OECD average. In the Philippines, the share of students below minimum proficiency fell by 11 percentage points in reading and 10 in science compared with 2018. The authors link the progress to reforms such as remedial programmes, structured foundational teaching and teacher support, while noting that PISA cannot show exactly which efforts caused the gains.

title: President Murmu lauds Akshaya Patra Foundation for 5 billion meals milestone, stresses nutrition and education for children
blurb: President Droupadi Murmu said nutritious food and quality education for children are a collective responsibility of teachers, parents, civil society, the corporate sector and government. Speaking at an event marking five billion school meals served by a mid-day meal charity over 25 years, she called the milestone remarkable. She noted that school meal programmes such as PM POSHAN have improved enrolment, attendance and retention, and that studies show better learning outcomes from improved nutrition. She added that such efforts complement the aims of Samagra Shiksha and the vision of a developed India by 2047.

title: NCERT introduces module on Computational Thinking and Artificial Intelligence for grades 9-12
blurb: NCERT has developed an introductory module on Computational Thinking and Artificial Intelligence for the Secondary Stage, Grades 9 to 12, in line with the National Education Policy 2020. Designed for students with no prior knowledge of AI, it presents computational thinking as a systematic approach to solving problems and explains how AI works, along with its applications, possibilities and limitations. The module uses discussions, practical exercises, experimentation and reflection, and its activities can be run with or without digital devices. It stresses ethical and safe use of AI, covering data privacy, misinformation, fairness and digital safety, while keeping human judgement and responsibility central.

title: Measures to Expand Access to Education
blurb: The Ministry of Education has set out measures to widen access to schooling, citing dropout rates from the Unified District Information System for Education Plus (UDISE+). The release outlines the steps taken under national schemes to keep children enrolled and learning across school stages. It presents the data as a reference point for continued efforts on retention and inclusion.

title: Gender and education: What is the latest data and evidence? | Global Education Monitoring Report
blurb: UNESCO's 2026 Gender Report and its Africa edition, which accompany the Global Education Monitoring Report, find that gender parity in enrolment was reached globally from pre-primary to upper secondary by 2024. Of 273 million out-of-school children, adolescents and youth in 2024, 140 million were boys and 133 million girls, and in Africa the girls' out-of-school rate fell from 47% to 28% between 2000 and 2024. Gaps persist within countries: in India, parity in upper secondary completion was reached in urban areas, but rural areas had 59 girls completing for every 100 boys. The reports recommend combined action on financial, social and educational barriers.

title: PISA testing: Every third fifteen-year-old in Serbia is functionally illiterate
blurb: Results of the 2025 PISA cycle show that students in Serbia scored lower than in the previous 2022 cycle. Among fifteen-year-olds, 53 percent fall below the functional literacy threshold in mathematics, 48 percent in reading and 43 percent in natural sciences. The report describes roughly every third student as functionally illiterate. Serbian students also trail peers in comparison countries by more than one school year, which the coverage presents as a widening educational gap.

title: Why education needs an AI evaluation layer | Hindustan Times
blurb: The author argues that AI-assisted assessment can turn student answers into evidence of reasoning, misconceptions and learning gaps, rather than only producing a score. Citing OECD TALIS 2024 data, the piece notes that teachers spend about 9% of their working time marking, and 40% report excessive marking as a source of stress. It says AI can handle first-pass evaluation of descriptive answers and pattern analysis while teachers retain judgement and final decisions. The author suggests building this assessment infrastructure to support competency-based examination in line with NEP 2020.

title: UN Report Highlights Mounting Challenges Facing Afghanistan’s Education System
blurb: A joint UNESCO and UNICEF Afghanistan Education Situation Report 2026, released on October 20, describes a widening gap between demand for education and the system's capacity. It says more than 2.6 million girls have been out of secondary school since 2021, while religious schools grew from 1,127 in 2019 to about 20,700 in 2025. A 2025 assessment of over 55,000 fourth-grade pupils found 43.5% reached minimum proficiency in language and 25.4% in mathematics, with girls outperforming boys in both. The report points to population growth, returning families and funding shortages as added pressures.

title: The Lean Education Manifesto; A Synthesis of 900+ Systematic Reviews for Visible Learning in Developing Countries
blurb: The Lean Education Manifesto brings together findings from more than 900 systematic reviews to identify what supports visible learning in developing countries. It offers a synthesis of the evidence base intended to help education systems focus on approaches with the strongest support.

title: AI for the last-minute question paper: A plug for exam leaks?
blurb: Nandan Nilekani, who heads the Centre's task force on examination reforms, has suggested using AI to assemble question papers shortly before an exam so that leaks become less rewarding, along with wider computer-based testing. A Parliamentary Standing Committee has likewise recommended a large, regularly updated question bank with papers put together close to the exam. Experts quoted say AI is best used to help specialists build a verified question bank, with encrypted digital delivery, comparable paper sets, audits and equal access for all candidates.

title: National Nutrition and Food Environment Report in Lebanese Public Schools
blurb: Lebanon has published its first national assessment of nutrition and food environments in public schools, drawing on data from 528 schools, 6,712 students and 4,449 families. It finds low dietary diversity, with 57 percent of students not meeting global dietary recommendations, alongside rising overweight and obesity and wide availability of unhealthy foods around schools. Nearly one in five students reported having no snack or money for food during the school day. Students in schools with a school meals programme were more likely to meet dietary recommendations, and the report calls for coordinated policy action across ministries.

title: UNESCO and UNICEF: 53% of Children in Afghanistan Lack Access to Formal Education
blurb: UNESCO and UNICEF have announced that 53% of children in Afghanistan lack access to formal education.

title: Big Tech in classrooms: Why parents should question Silicon Valley’s growing influence on education
blurb: The piece asks how much influence technology companies should have over what children learn as Big Tech products become more common in classrooms. It encourages parents to question the growing role of Silicon Valley firms in shaping school education.

title: Small AI, Big Learning Possibilities
blurb: A World Bank Group feature describes how small AI tools, meaning practical and affordable technology built for a specific local need, are being piloted to support teachers and students. In Ethiopia, the AI-Coach app lets teachers record lessons and receive feedback on student engagement, questioning and instructional quality, and it works on phones with intermittent connectivity. The pilot reached close to 350 English and mathematics teachers, who found the feedback timely, tailored and practical. The Bank is working with countries on similar tools that personalise learning and guide students' career choices, as 1.2 billion young people are projected to enter the workforce in developing countries over the next decade.

title: Accountability in Education: What Works? Case Studies from Simbu
blurb: This World Bank case study, part of the series Accountability in Education: What Works?, examines the rise of women in education leadership in Simbu, Papua New Guinea, over the last two decades. It links the trend to merit-based appointments and promotions, noting that patronage systems elsewhere are largely dominated by men. The study discusses what drove the change and draws on interviews with past and present senior officials and education stakeholders about why it matters. It notes that schools offer women significant leadership opportunities even where political leadership remains limited.

title: The MND Mexico Well-being Series, Part 2: Education
blurb: A data review compares Mexico with other countries on eight education indicators, drawing mainly on OECD Education at a Glance 2026 figures. In early childhood education, only 4% of two-year-olds in Mexico were enrolled in programmes combining education and care in 2024, against an OECD average of 50%. Among children aged 3 to the start of primary school, 75% were enrolled, compared with an OECD average of 90%, placing Mexico 42nd of 46 countries. The review notes that about 84% of primary and secondary students attend public schools, and that experiences vary with the resources and teaching staff available.

title: Micro Skills in Bangladesh Secondary Schools
blurb: Bangladesh has widened access to secondary education, but many adolescents leave school without practical skills. This UNICEF working paper reviews the first year of the Micro Skills programme in 120 secondary schools, reaching an estimated 16,000 students through career planning, digital learning and safety, social-emotional learning and green skills. It finds that 82 per cent of students felt better prepared for their future, though 57 per cent attended four sessions or fewer. The paper sets out seven priorities for the next phase, including better attendance, teacher training and support, narrowing gender gaps, and exploring integration into the formal curriculum.

title: Enhancing teacher productivity with information on students and skills: experimental evidence from Bangladesh
source: What Works Hub for Global Education
blurb: A randomised evaluation in 312 schools in Bangladesh tested giving Grade-6 maths teachers results from two brief tests, reports flagging topics and students needing support, and an annotated answer key. At baseline, teachers could not estimate their students' scores or class rank, and interacted twice as often with high- as with low-achieving students. The programme raised maths achievement by 0.23 standard deviations and reading by 0.17, with similar gains across the baseline distribution, and improved three social-emotional skills. Teachers also spread interactions more evenly and stressed more foundational content. At $5.06 per student, the study shows that making use of existing exam data can raise teacher productivity cheaply.

title: High-Powered Task Force Invites Suggestions on Reforms in Public Examinations
blurb: The Government of India has constituted a High-Powered Task Force, with Shri Nandan Nilekani as its head, to look at reforms in public examinations. The Task Force is inviting suggestions from stakeholders and the public to help shape improvements in how examinations are conducted. Interested citizens, educators and institutions can submit their views through the channel announced by the Press Information Bureau.

title: Accessible Textbooks for Every Child
blurb: This UNICEF learning brief reviews implementation research on Accessible Digital Textbooks, which help governments adapt curriculum-aligned textbooks into flexible formats with audio narration, sign-language videos, simplified text and image descriptions. It notes that nearly 240 million children worldwide live with disabilities and that those aged 10 to 17 are 49 per cent more likely to have never attended school. The brief recommends involving children, teachers and persons with disabilities in design and testing, giving teachers practical training, and ensuring devices, connectivity and technical support. It also calls for further research on learning impact and on the costs of AI-assisted production.

title: More than half of primary school-age children in Afghanistan outside
blurb: UNESCO reports that more than half of primary school-age children in Afghanistan are outside school. The finding highlights the scale of the country's out-of-school challenge at the primary level.

title: PARAKH Plans Monthly Assessments to Address Learning Gaps in Schools
blurb: PARAKH, the assessment unit under NCERT, has proposed a five-stage monthly cycle of classroom interventions and competency-based assessments to act on findings from PARAKH Rashtriya Sarvekshan 2024. The framework was presented to more than 600 state and district officials in workshops held in New Delhi between September 18 and 30. The survey covered over 21.15 lakh students in 74,229 schools across 781 districts and showed average mathematics scores moving from 60 per cent in Class 3 to 37 per cent in Class 9. Teachers would use focused lessons and remedial practice, with short monthly assessments and stage-appropriate, play-based approaches at the foundational stage.

title: Foundational Learning Action Tracker 2026: Results for Africa
blurb: The 2026 Foundational Learning Action Tracker covers 52 African countries, with survey data from 37, and monitors national efforts to accelerate foundational learning using the RAPID Framework. This edition focuses on assessments as a system-wide enabler. Among countries with survey data, about 7 in 10 report using assessment data nationwide for policy and planning, but only about 4 in 10 use it to inform classroom practice in all schools. The tracker also finds that countries continue to adopt supportive policies, and that stronger systems are needed to implement, sustain and monitor them.

title: Vendor payments CBSE | India News
blurb: In reply to a Right to Information application filed on August 22, CBSE said on October 14 that its finance section has not yet received a sanction order for payment to Coempt Edu Teck, the vendor for the on-screen marking system used in the 2026 Class 12 board examinations. The board's finance department also said it holds no information on penalties imposed on the company. CBSE officials had said in June that the vendor would be penalised for shortcomings in the evaluation system, which drew student complaints about scanned answer sheets and technical issues after the results were announced on May 13.

title: PARAKH rolls out monthly district-level interventions to address learning gaps | India News
blurb: PARAKH, the national assessment centre within NCERT, has rolled out a nationwide plan for monthly, competency-based teaching and assessment to act on learning gaps found in the PARAKH Rashtriya Sarvekshan 2024. The framework was presented to more than 600 state and district education officials from all states and Union territories at workshops in New Delhi from September 18 to 30. It envisages action plans across 781 districts, in which officials identify weak competencies, set monthly learning targets and track progress through periodic assessments. The approach treats survey results as diagnostic signals, shifting the focus from measuring performance to improving it.

title: Is effort aversion holding your students back?
blurb: A UNSW Sydney study on effort aversion finds that some people feel the cost of effort more sharply than others, enough to turn down a larger reward to avoid it. A 15-minute measure of effort motivation predicted university grades across two terms, and proved a stronger predictor than students' own sense of how much they procrastinate. In a separate experiment, learners who believed a lecture came from a real person felt more connected to the lecturer and were keener to learn more. The lead researcher suggests schools can reward effort and role-model persistence.

title: Innovative approaches to climate education among adolescents and youths in Eastern and Southern Africa
blurb: This research looks at innovative approaches to climate education among adolescents and youths in Eastern and Southern Africa. It explores how schools and communities can turn climate education into practical, engaging experiences that empower young people to take climate action.

title: Showing Up: A Diagnostic of Primary Education in Somalia
blurb: A World Bank Group diagnostic titled Showing Up examines primary education in Somalia. The report reviews the state of the country's primary school system and is intended to inform education planning and policy for that system.

title: Learning-by-Doing at Home: The Childhood Origins of Girls’ Domestic Work
blurb: This job market paper from the London School of Economics studies how girls' domestic work takes shape in rural India. Using rainfall-driven variation in household-production demand, it finds that a one-standard-deviation rainfall increase at ages 4-7 raises girls' domestic work at ages 12-17 by 5.3 minutes a day, against an insignificant 1.0 minute for boys. The effect is concentrated among eldest daughters, and their households obtain 4-10 percent more consumption per minute. Despite lower study time, the paper finds little evidence of adverse effects on enrolment, grade progression or measured learning.

title: NCERT plans multilingual training programme for future teachers
blurb: NCERT is developing a multilingual teacher training model to prepare undergraduate, postgraduate and research students at its university to teach more than one language in schools. The programmes will pair language proficiency with the pedagogical skills needed to handle several languages in a classroom. The aim is to help schools widen the range of languages offered, especially where too few students opt for a language to justify a separate teacher. Details such as the number of languages per teacher, proficiency levels, timeline, admission criteria and course duration are yet to be finalised, and the proposal aligns with the multilingualism emphasis of NEP 2020.

title: IIT Delhi, Lithuania train nearly 300 schoolgirls in ethical AI
blurb: Nearly 300 schoolgirls have completed an online artificial intelligence training programme delivered in India for the first time in 2026, covering AI foundations, ethical use and the role of women in technology. A concluding event in Delhi featured a panel on AI and the future of education, along with sessions on responsible AI use and building ethics into AI design. The programme aims to familiarise young women with AI and encourage their participation in STEM, where women remain under-represented across research, development and leadership. Organisers noted that its longer-term impact will depend on whether students build on the introductory training through further study.

title: Inside the silence zone: How noise pollution near schools impacts students' health and education
blurb: A feature examines how noise near schools affects learning, drawing on a study published in the Journal of the Association of Environmental and Resource Economists in August 2026 that linked ambient noise data with Class 12 examination outcomes across six Indian cities. Daytime noise near schools exceeded 55 dB on nearly 87 per cent of days during board-exam preparation and examinations, and a 10-percentage-point rise in noisy days was associated with a 2.3 per cent higher failure rate among boys. A March 2026 UNICEF report calls environmental noise a preventable hazard for children, and experts suggest soundproofing, better classroom design and combined indoor and outdoor noise assessments.

title: UNESCO Calls for Responsible Use of Technology in Schools and Universities
blurb: UNESCO has urged governments and education authorities to take a balanced approach to digital learning, saying technology should support classroom teaching rather than replace interaction between teachers and students. Revisiting its 2023 GEM Report, Technology in Education: A Tool on Whose Terms?, it asks policymakers to base decisions on learners' needs, the quality of evidence and the resources needed to sustain digital systems. It outlines four tests for any tool: whether it is appropriate for the learning objective, equitable, scalable and sustainable. It also flags unequal internet access, privacy risks and insufficient training as major challenges.

title: Why is strong education leadership needed to revive progress towards SDG 4?
blurb: The 2024/5 Global Education Monitoring Report, Lead for learning, calls for greater investment in education leaders from school to system level to revive progress towards SDG 4. It says more than a quarter of the variation in schools' learning levels is attributable to principals, yet a study in 14 low- and middle-income countries found administration takes two thirds of their time. Only around three in ten countries require principals to have management experience, and fewer than two thirds have competitive recruitment for principals. The report recommends fair selection, support for professional growth and shared leadership involving teachers, students and communities.

title: What are appropriate uses of technology in education?
blurb: The sixth GEM Report, Technology in education: A tool on whose terms?, urges countries to set their own terms for how technology is designed and used so that it supports rather than replaces teacher-led instruction. It offers policymakers a four-point compass and notes that learning benefits fade when technology is overused or used without a qualified teacher, while fewer than a quarter of countries ban smartphones in schools. Only 11 of 51 governments surveyed have AI curricula, and basic digital learning plus school connectivity in lower-income countries would add 50% to their SDG 4 financing gap. The report calls for national school internet connectivity benchmarks by 2030.

title: Austerity and privatization weakened OECD education systems
blurb: A commentary on the OECD PISA 2025 results, which recorded the lowest averages ever measured across the OECD in reading, mathematics and science, argues that the decline began well before AI and social media and followed austerity reforms after 2008. It says half of OECD countries cut or froze teacher salaries after 2010, and primary teachers in 13 OECD countries and economies earned less in real terms in 2024 than in 2015. The share of students in schools reporting that teacher shortages hinder instruction rose from 26% in 2018 to 47% in 2022. It also notes that 17% of teachers intend to leave within five years.

title: NIOS bridge course registration reopens on October 21; BEd-qualified teachers can apply till October 28
blurb: The National Institute of Open Schooling is reopening registration for its six-month certificate bridge course in primary teacher education on October 21. Teachers who hold a BEd qualification are eligible to apply, and application forms can be submitted until October 28. Candidates apply online through the official bridge course website, bridge.nios.ac.in. They are advised to fill in their personal and professional details accurately, then download the confirmation page and keep a printout for future reference.

title: NCERT Plans New Course To Train Teachers To Teach Multiple Languages | Exclusive | Education and Career News
blurb: NCERT is planning a new course to train teachers to teach in multiple languages. The initiative relates to multilingual teaching in schools and the preparation of teachers for classrooms where more than one language is used, in line with the focus on mother-tongue and multilingual education.

title: PM CARES for Children Scheme: Aadhaar authentication mandatory for scholarship benefits, no child to be d
blurb: The Centre has made Aadhaar authentication, or proof of possession of an Aadhaar number, necessary for children seeking scholarship benefits under the PM CARES for Children Scheme. At the same time, no child will be denied assistance if they do not have an Aadhaar number or are unable to complete authentication, and alternative verification is permitted where authentication does not succeed. Beneficiaries aged 18 and above are asked to provide documents including a Class 10 or Class 12 certificate or marks statement issued by a recognised school education board.

title: Is your five-year-old ready for Class 1, or is preschool still important? UNESCO report raises a question Indian parents cannot ignore
blurb: Coverage of UNESCO's 2026 Global Education Monitoring Report highlights that 51% of five-year-olds in India are enrolled in primary rather than pre-primary education. The report notes that children already in primary school may be counted as participating in organised learning, which can overstate early-education coverage; globally, 27% of children one year below primary entry age are in primary school. The article says school readiness is about communication, social and emotional skills and play-based experiences, in line with the National Curriculum Framework, rather than early reading or writing.

title: THE GAP BETWEEN BUDGET AND EXPENDITURE IN INDIAN SCHOOL EDUCATION SYSTEM
blurb: This study examines the gap between budget allocation and actual expenditure in Indian school education from 2018-19 to 2023-24, using secondary data from official government sources and trend, comparative and ranking analysis. It finds that despite a significant rise in budget allocations, an expenditure gap persists, with the COVID-19 period showing the largest gap and notable regional differences in fund utilisation. The author recommends stronger financial governance, more efficient fund use and better administrative mechanisms to support quality education, in line with SDG 4 and Viksit Bharat 2047.

title: With Another Bill On Anvil, Should Education Return To The State List?
blurb: The author asks whether education should return to the State List, noting it has been on the Concurrent List since 1976. States account for about 73.2 per cent of budgeted education spending, while central laws and national schemes shape much of what they do. The piece links this to the cancelled and re-held NEET-UG exam and the Viksit Bharat Shiksha Adhishthan Bill, 2025. It suggests defining more precisely where national uniformity is needed and where states should have room to decide.

title: Department of School Education and Literacy focuses on administrative efficiency, cleaner school campuses and responsible e-waste Management as part of Special Campaign 6
blurb: The Department of School Education and Literacy in the Union Ministry of Education is taking part in Special Campaign 6.0. Its focus areas are administrative efficiency, cleaner school campuses and responsible management of e-waste. The update presents these efforts as part of the Ministry's continuing work on better-run and well-maintained school environments.

title: NCERT To Organise Live Sessions On Dyslexia-Friendly Classrooms From October 19
blurb: NCERT will hold a series of live sessions on creating dyslexia-friendly classrooms, starting on October 19.

title: U.S. Teens Rank 23rd In Math, 10th In Reading On The 2026 Global Exam
blurb: Coverage of the 2025 PISA results, released on 8 September, reports that US 15-year-olds tied for 10th in reading and 23rd in math among 91 school systems. Reading scores across rich countries fell 28 points between 2015 and 2025, and one in five 15-year-olds now misses the basic skill level in all three subjects, up from 16% in 2022. The OECD notes the decline in reading began before the pandemic in many countries.

title: Why competency development needs to begin in school
blurb: The author argues that the foundations of employability already exist in everyday school learning, such as problem solving in mathematics, evidence-based questioning in science and critical reading, and that they can be developed more deliberately. He notes that syllabus completion and exams leave little room for this, so benefits often depend on individual students' initiative. He suggests a separate, low-cost track for foundational competencies that does not add a new syllabus, ideally beginning between ages 12 and 14, to help students prepare for changing workplace needs.

title: One teacher, multiple languages: NCERT eyes new training model
