blurb: NCERT is exploring a new training model under which a single teacher would be prepared to teach in multiple languages. The plan is linked to the emphasis that National Education Policy 2020 places on multilingualism in schools.

title: Student life of a homeschooled child
blurb: A student writes in The Hindu about moving to the National Institute of Open Schooling (NIOS) for Classes 11 and 12 after being asked to repeat a year at her school. She describes online admission needing only the Class 10 marksheet and identity documents, the freedom to choose subjects, study centre and exam centre, and the Personal Contact Programme classes where doubts are cleared with teachers. Early months of self-study were hard, but she says the format built discipline. Other NIOS students quoted describe flexible schedules and subject choices that suited their college plans.

title: India’s Missing Human Capital: The Gender Gap in Education-to-Work Transitions
blurb: An ORF analysis notes that about 87 million young Indians, one in four, were not in employment, education or training (NEET) in 2025, and that ILO data from 2022 found young women five times more likely than young men to be NEET. Girls now match or outperform boys in school enrolment, transition and completion, so the gap has shifted to the move from education into work. About 88 percent of NEET young women do unpaid domestic and care work, and female labour-force participation ranges from 80.9 percent in Hamirpur to 18.9 percent in East Delhi. The piece calls for policies that help women convert their skills into productive, better-quality work.

title: Teaching students to think in the age of ChatGPT
blurb: Writing in The Hindu, ELT resource person Albert P'Rayan argues that AI does not by itself decide whether students think; what matters is how it is used. Starting from a child who wanted to ask ChatGPT why women like pink, he says children must learn that AI does not have every answer. He calls claims that AI kills creativity and critical thinking largely myths, while warning that shortcuts can bypass the process of learning. He recommends clear institutional AI policies, teacher training to redesign assessment around higher-order thinking, teaching students to verify AI output, and large-scale research on AI's effect on learning.

title: School urges social media curbs for children, SC seeks response from govt, child rights panel
blurb: A Supreme Court Bench of Chief Justice Surya Kant and Justice Joymalya Bagchi has sought responses from the Centre and the National Commission for Protection of Child Rights on a plea from Emerald Heights International School, Indore, seeking curbs on children's social media use. The petition describes students preoccupied with likes and appearance, along with sleep loss, anxiety and low self-esteem. It notes that platforms set a self-declared minimum age of 13, while the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 treats under-18s as children needing verifiable parental consent. The school asks for a national framework that starts with reliable, privacy-preserving age assurance at account creation.

title: Stronger Law, Safer Exams: India Tightens the Noose on Paper Leaks
blurb: The Government has introduced the Public Examinations (Prevention of Unfair Means) Amendment Bill, 2026 in the Lok Sabha to strengthen the 2024 law against paper leaks. The Bill raises jail terms and fines, including fines of up to Rs 5 crore and bans of up to eight years from conducting public examinations. The Centre may set up dedicated Special Task Forces, and investigations must finish within two months. Each State and UT must designate Special Fast Track Courts that hear cases day to day and complete trials within three months of the chargesheet, with appeals going to a two-judge High Court bench.

title: Govt ropes in aided, private teachers, PSU staff for Census work
blurb: The Times of India reports that the Union government has widened the pool of people who can be deployed for Census work. Teachers from aided and unaided private schools and staff of public sector undertakings and banks can now be assigned alongside government school teachers.

title: A snapshot of America’s schools: Trends and global comparisons
blurb: Brookings has published a data snapshot of trends in American schools and how they compare internationally. A footnote cites an estimate that prior trends explain 44% of the post-COVID decline in 4th grade maths and reading. The headline findings were not available.

title: Gender Inclusion Fund Under NEP 2020: Bridging Gender Gaps In Education
source: IMPRI Impact and Policy Research Institute
blurb: An IMPRI policy brief examines the Gender Inclusion Fund (GIF) under NEP 2020, which aims to expand equitable access to quality education for girls and transgender students. It explains that the GIF is meant to address barriers such as cost, safety, distance, menstrual hygiene and stereotypes through measures like sanitation facilities, bicycles, conditional cash transfers and community interventions. The Ministry of Education says these goals are being pursued through Samagra Shiksha 2.0 provisions, including free textbooks and uniforms, residential schooling, self-defence training and stipends. UDISE+ data cited show girls' secondary GER rising from 79.4% to 80.1% between 2021-22 and 2022-23.

title: The curriculum of control: How CBSE teaches children to conform, not question
blurb: In a Deccan Herald opinion piece, Navneet Sharma and Ashu Sharma argue that CBSE's life-skills and wellbeing material, used in more than 33,000 schools, treats ordinary adolescent traits such as curiosity and rebellion as risk factors. They acknowledge units on self-awareness, empathy and safe touch, but say sexuality is framed mainly through infections and opposite-sex attraction. They also say an older Adolescence Education Programme case study lists a victim's lack of assertiveness under responsibility for abuse and remains in the resource library. The authors suggest the material should do more to support adolescent agency and critical thinking.

title: Ministry of Women and Child Development launches Rashtriya Poshan Maah 2026: Nationwide campaign focuses on dietary diversity, adequate protein intake and fresh hot cooked meals
blurb: The Ministry of Women and Child Development launched the 9th Rashtriya Poshan Maah 2026 in Varanasi on 9 September, a month-long nutrition campaign themed "Hamari Anganwadi, Hamari Jimmedari". It focuses on dietary diversity, adequate protein and fresh hot cooked meals. Union Minister Annpurna Devi said over 14 lakh Anganwadi Centres serve more than 7.5 crore children, 1.10 crore pregnant and lactating women and nearly 16 lakh adolescent girls, and that 2 lakh centres are being upgraded to Saksham Anganwadis. She noted that PMMVY has transferred over Rs 21,000 crore to more than 4.65 crore mothers, and called for nutrition to become a Jan Andolan.

title: Centre asks nodal officers to ensure timely verification of NMMSS scholarship applications
blurb: The Department of School Education and Literacy has asked state, district and institute nodal officers to verify National Means-cum-Merit Scholarship Scheme applications accurately and on time. The scheme gives Rs 12,000 a year to meritorious students from economically weaker sections to reduce dropout after Class VIII. Registration on the National Scholarship Portal for 2026-27 closes on October 31, 2026, with institute- and district-level verification due by November 15 and November 30. The guidance followed a regional review workshop in Bhopal on October 14, led by Economic Adviser A. Srija, where states shared implementation experiences.

title: CIC asks CBSE to conduct surprise checks over alleged dummy school admissions
blurb: The Central Information Commission has recommended under Section 25(5) of the RTI Act that CBSE carry out surprise inspections of affiliated schools to check for dummy admissions and compliance with attendance rules. The order by Information Commissioner Sudha Rani Relangi came on a complaint about private schools in Bhopal, where students were allegedly enrolled while attending coaching centres instead of classes. CBSE's Affiliation Bye-Laws, 2018 bar schools from presenting students who do not meet attendance requirements for board exams. The recommendation does not establish wrongdoing by any school; CBSE inspections at 29 schools in January 2025 had found irregularities.

title: ‘From assuming to knowing’: How impact evaluations support the design, delivery, and scale-up of school meal programs
blurb: An IFPRI piece discusses how impact evaluations can support the design, delivery and scale-up of school meal programmes, moving from assumptions to evidence.

title: Private school teachers can be deployed for Census work: RGI
blurb: The Centre amended the Census Rules, 1990 on October 16, allowing states and UTs to appoint teachers of aided or unaided private institutions, as well as staff of PSUs, banks and other bodies, as Census enumerators. The gazette notification was issued by Registrar General of India Mrityunjay Kumar Narayan. It follows a Punjab and Haryana High Court petition by private schools, in which an October 8 order stayed Haryana's requisition of their teachers; the case is listed for April 29, 2027. Census 2027, approved at Rs 11,718 crore, is being conducted in two phases.

title: Govt issues notification on PM CARES scholarship, spells out rules for children without Aadhaar
blurb: The Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment notified Aadhaar authentication rules on 14 October 2026 for the PM CARES for Children scholarship, which supports education from Class 1 to 12. The notification says no child can be denied benefits solely because Aadhaar authentication fails or they have no Aadhaar number. Children without Aadhaar can use an enrolment acknowledgement plus documents such as a birth certificate or school certificate, while those facing biometric failures can use OTP or offline QR-code verification. A designated officer will verify documents, and records of alternative verification for children will be audited periodically.

title: Centre expands Census enumerator pool to include private school teachers, clerks
blurb: The Times of India reports that the Centre has expanded the pool of people eligible to serve as Census enumerators to include private school teachers and clerks.

title: Australian primary students taught basic maths two years later than overseas peers, study reveals
blurb: The Australian reports on a study finding that Australian primary students are taught basic maths about two years later than their peers in other countries.

title: CIC flags alleged dummy admissions, recommends surprise checks at CBSE-affiliated schools
blurb: The Central Information Commission has flagged alleged dummy admissions and recommended that CBSE carry out surprise inspections of its affiliated schools. The aim is to check compliance with mandatory attendance rules and strengthen checks on affiliation conditions.

title: School meals are one of the keys to improving access and equity in education
blurb: A post on UNESCO's World Education Blog argues that school meals are one of the keys to improving access and equity in education.

title: FutureReady Schools: What Does ‘Being Prepared for Tomorrow’ Really Mean?
blurb: An ORF concept note for a stakeholder discussion asks whether a future-ready school is defined by smart classrooms, coding and robotics, or by the capabilities it builds in students, teachers and leaders. It argues that generative AI makes the question urgent and that schools may need to develop critical thinking, evidence evaluation, collaboration, responsible AI use and judgement. The discussion aims to identify enablers and barriers across curriculum, assessment, teacher development, technology and partnerships. It seeks shared, context-sensitive principles that align with equity and inclusion, including which skills students should graduate with by 2030.

title: Closing India’s foundational literacy gap | Hindustan Times
blurb: Writing in the Hindustan Times, Room to Read India country director Poornima Garg argues that many children can decode words but not read for meaning, an issue central to planning for NIPUN 2.0. She cites PARAKH Rashtriya Sarvekshan 2024, where Grade 3 children averaged 64% in language but 60% in reading comprehension. She calls this a translation challenge rather than a policy one, pointing to a children's book market of only Rs 720 crore with few Indian-language stories, and a system geared to completing the syllabus. She recommends aligning assessments, textbooks and teacher preparation around reading, supported by storytelling and read-alouds.

title: Nearly half of all students enrolled in IIT Madras’ school outreach initiative are girls
blurb: The Indian Express reports that nearly half of the students enrolled in IIT Madras's school outreach initiative are girls. The institute aims to expand the programme to 25,000 schools from its current network of 6,406 partner schools.

title: UNESCO Reports Global Education Parity from Preschool to Secondary
blurb: UNESCO's 2026 Gender Report finds that girls and boys are now equally enrolled worldwide from preschool through secondary school, with 50 million more girls enrolled since 2015. Completion rates rose from 86 to 89 percent in primary, 74 to 79 percent in lower secondary and 54 to 61 percent in upper secondary, yet 122 million girls remain out of school. Early marriage and pregnancy remain major barriers; 16 Sub-Saharan countries have adopted or strengthened return policies for young mothers. The report notes that in India urban areas show parity while rural areas stand at 59 girls per 100 boys in one completion measure.

title: What you need to know about mental health and psychosocial support in schools
blurb: This UNESCO explainer sets out why mental health and psychosocial support belongs in and through schools. It notes that one in seven adolescents aged 10-19 experiences a mental health condition, and that children who are bullied are twice as likely to feel lonely, struggle to sleep and have considered suicide. A comprehensive approach combines promotion and prevention for all learners, early support for those in difficulty and access to appropriate care. It also highlights that gender, disability and background shape how learners experience these challenges, and that teachers need support for their own wellbeing too.

title: Centre pushes open schooling via NIOS to achieve 100% enrolment by 2030
blurb: The Department of School Education and Literacy will strengthen open schooling through NIOS to bring out-of-school children back and reach 100 per cent GER by 2030, in line with NEP 2020. It cites PLFS 2023-24 data showing nearly 2 crore children aged 14-18 out of school, and over 50 lakh students failing board exams each year. States and UTs will run a nationwide drive using district survey data, and the NIOS Mitra programme will deploy trained facilitators to enrol and support marginalised learners. NIOS, with over 10,800 centres, aims for at least one centre per block, using PM SHRI schools, KVs and JNVs.

title: UDISE+ report shows rise in teachers, fall in school dropout rates
blurb: The Ministry of Education's UDISE+ 2025-26 report shows teacher numbers rising 8.3 per cent to 1,02,73,020 from 94,83,294 in 2022-23, with pupil-teacher ratios of 10 to 21 across stages, better than the NEP norm of 30:1. Secondary dropout fell from 8.2 to 7 per cent and secondary GER rose from 68.5 to 71.7 per cent. Single-teacher schools fell to 1,00,843 and zero-enrolment schools dropped about 29 per cent to 5,663. Computer access rose to 69.9 per cent and internet to 67.4 per cent of schools, while women made up 54.9 per cent of teachers.

title: Learning at the Speed of AI: Using Platform Trials to Test AI Innovation
blurb: A Center for Global Development publication looks at how platform trials could be used to test AI innovations quickly and rigorously, an approach of interest for evidence-based education technology.

title: From assessment to the classroom: using data to improve learning in the Dominican Republic
blurb: UNESCO reports that its Latin American Laboratory for Assessment of the Quality of Education (LLECE) held three workshops in Santiago de los Caballeros and Santo Domingo to help teachers and school leaders turn assessment results into classroom action. The workshops focused on using ERCE Schools assessments as a formative tool to identify where students need support and adjust teaching. Carmen Taveras of the Dominican Ministry of Education said the project began with 30 institutions and has scaled to 54 in its second stage. LLECE coordinator Carlos Henriquez also visited schools and met officials to plan next steps.

title: Google extends AI teacher training to Bihar, Madhya Pradesh and Sikkim
blurb: Google is extending its AI Educator Series through new partnerships with Bihar, Madhya Pradesh, Sikkim and the Ministry of Skill Development and Entrepreneurship, after more than 80,000 educators completed it since its May 2026 launch in India. The free, self-paced, NEP-aligned training covers tools such as Gemini and NotebookLM for lesson planning and learning materials. Bihar signed a Statement of Intent in September for training in Hindi and English, while Sikkim's October 6 agreement covers faculty at 15 government colleges and Khangchendzonga State University. Versions in six more Indian languages are expected later in October.

title: Three-Day Capacity Building Programme for Nodal School Principals and School Leaders on NEP 2020 and NCF-SE 2023 Concludes at RIE Bhubaneswar
blurb: A three-day capacity building programme on NEP 2020 and NCF-SE 2023 for nodal school principals and school leaders has concluded at the Regional Institute of Education (RIE), Bhubaneswar. The programme was aimed at equipping school leaders to take forward the national education policy and the school curriculum framework. Further details of the sessions were not available in the source.

title: Ministry of Education organises Orientation-cum-Review Workshop on National Means-cum-Merit Scholarship Scheme (NMMSS) to Strengthen Scholarship Implementation and Verification Processes
blurb: The Ministry of Education held an orientation-cum-review workshop on the National Means-cum-Merit Scholarship Scheme (NMMSS). The workshop was intended to strengthen how the scholarship is implemented and how applications are verified. Further details, such as participants or specific decisions, were not available in the source.

title: NCERT brings personal finance to Class 9, but can one chapter build money habits?
blurb: NCERT's new Class 9 Social Science textbook, released on 28 September, includes a chapter titled Managing Your Personal Finances, covering income, budgeting, saving, investing, and protection and risk management, along with EMIs and income-tax calculations. The chapter builds on economic themes introduced in the Class 6 and 7 textbooks and, being in mainstream Social Science, reaches students across all streams. Trainers and experts quoted say lasting habits will depend on enough classroom time, hands-on activities and parental involvement. The article also notes a CISCE teacher handbook recommending that financial literacy be integrated across subjects in Classes VI–X rather than taught as a standalone subject.

title: Nilekani suggests AI-made exams: China prints papers in prisons, other countries use question banks to stop leaks | HT Explainers
blurb: Nandan Nilekani, who heads an examination reforms committee, proposed on October 13 that question papers be generated by AI from a large question bank on the day of the test, removing the incentive to sell a leaked paper, and called for expanding computer-based testing beyond India's 150,000 test locations. The proposal follows the cancellation of this year's NEET-UG after a paper leak. The explainer compares global practice: computer tests such as the SAT and MCAT use pretested question banks and multiple forms, while China's gaokao and South Korea's Suneung isolate paper-setters until the exam and use tightly secured printing and transport.

title: OECD official hails Türkiye's 2025 PISA results as a 'success story'
blurb: OECD Director for Education and Skills Andreas Schleicher described Türkiye's PISA 2025 results as a success story worth close study. Türkiye is among the few countries where average performance in mathematics, reading and science rose between 2022 and 2025. The share of low-performing students has also fallen significantly since 2015. Schleicher noted that seven in ten students said their teachers take an interest in their learning and offer extra support, and that students reported a more positive classroom climate than a decade ago.

title: Education: A Pathway to Opportunity and Empowerment
blurb: A PIB feature released on 14 October 2026 by the Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment profiles Ajay Kumar Ahirwar, a 37-year-old Scheduled Caste research scholar working as Guest Faculty. Under the National Fellowship Scheme for Scheduled Caste Students (NFSC), he receives ₹31,000 per month, which covers research, study and living costs. The release says the support has eased financial pressure, letting him balance his job with continued research. It presents his experience as an example of how targeted fellowships help students from disadvantaged backgrounds pursue higher education and academic careers.

title: Every School, A Model School
blurb: A PIB feature titled ‘Every School, A Model School’ presents the Pradhan Mantri Schools for Rising India (PM SHRI) initiative, launched on 7 September 2022, as part of the effort to develop model schools under the National Education Policy.

title: Prime Minister highlights the strong contribution of teachers on Teachers' Day
blurb: A Press Information Bureau release reports that the Prime Minister highlighted the strong contribution of teachers on Teachers' Day.

title: As attacks on schools rise by 33% in 2025, UNESCO calls for stronger protection of education
blurb: UNESCO reports that the United Nations verified 1,680 attacks on schools in 2025, up 33% from 1,265 in 2024, alongside 38,558 grave violations against children, the highest since monitoring began. About 74 million out-of-school crisis-affected children live in 20 countries, and 74% of refugee children are out of school. UNESCO is working with partners in more than 20 countries on preparedness, learning continuity and recovery, from shelters in Ukraine to temporary learning spaces in Gaza, and its Executive Board adopted a Plan of Action to Protect Education from Attack in April 2026. It urges all parties to respect international law and the Safe Schools Declaration.

title: More children out of school for the 7th year in a row, up to 273 million
blurb: UNESCO's 2026 GEM Report finds that the number of out-of-school children has risen for a seventh year, reaching up to 273 million, as progress has slowed since 2015, especially in sub-Saharan Africa. It also documents gains: enrolment reached 1.4 billion in 2024, up 30% since 2000, and completion rates rose from 77% to 88% in primary and 37% to 61% in upper secondary. While 76% of countries reallocate resources to disadvantaged schools, only 8% use such mechanisms to full effect. The report recommends evidence-based, multi-angle policies, noting measurable gains linked to compulsory schooling, electrification and school feeding.

title: Safe learning environments: Preventing and addressing violence in and around school
blurb: This UNESCO evidence overview says school violence occurs in all countries: one in three learners is bullied every month, over 36% experience a physical fight with peers, and cyberbullying affects as many as one in ten children. Half of school-going children aged 6-17 live in countries where corporal punishment at school is not fully prohibited. It links violence to poorer physical and mental health and lower learning outcomes, and describes a holistic approach built on advocacy, global partnerships and guidance for countries, including global guidance on school-related gender-based violence and policy recommendations on ending bullying.

title: Open minds please: School can't teach children everything but must foster lifelong learning
blurb: The author uses discoveries about animal minds, such as Jane Goodall's tool-using chimpanzees, capuchin monkeys rejecting unfair rewards and elephants that appear to use names, to argue that once-settled scientific consensus can be confidently wrong. The piece says knowledge often advances at the edges between disciplines, so people should read widely and with an open mind. Since schools cannot teach everything and much content will later be revised, the author argues their lasting task is building dispositions for lifelong learning: stamina for long texts, holding views lightly, and the habit of asking why. The piece closes with a call for humility towards people unlike ourselves.

title: By rewriting textbooks, India is weakening spirit of enquiry mandated by the Constitution
blurb: The author argues that NCERT's new Class 9 social science textbook, which removes chapters on European revolutions and frames medieval Indian history around “Resistance and Resilience” against invasions, presents a simplified view that leaves out cultural exchanges such as the Sufi and Bhakti traditions. The piece links this to the constitutional duty to develop scientific temper and a spirit of enquiry, citing figures from Nehru to Meghnad Saha. It also cites the Free to Think 2026 report, which places India's Academic Freedom Index at 0.14 in 2025, down from 0.38 in 2022. The author calls for education that encourages questioning and critical thinking.

title: The out-of-school child: understanding educational exclusion in India
blurb: Shantha Sinha's article in Azim Premji University's Learning Curve (Issue 23, 2026, pp. 6–12) examines educational exclusion in India through the figure of the out-of-school child.

title: New UNESCO data released on World Teachers’ Day shows the world needs
blurb: New UNESCO data released ahead of World Teachers' Day show that 58% of global demand for teachers is driven by teachers leaving the profession, with annual attrition of 7.2% in pre-primary, 4.7% in primary and 5.4% in secondary education. In 27 of 68 countries analysed, teacher salaries are below those of similarly qualified professionals, and the primary pupil–teacher ratio is about 28 to 1. UNESCO is supporting teachers' digital and AI skills, and a Ministerial Statement adopted on 8 September 2026 says AI must support, not replace, teachers. The 5 October event in Paris marks 60 years of the Recommendation concerning the Status of Teachers.

title: New UNESCO data released on World Teachers’ Day shows the world needs 50 million additional teachers
blurb: New UNESCO data released around World Teachers' Day 2026 show 107 million teachers worldwide, with a further 50 million needed. About 58 per cent of that demand comes from teachers leaving the profession, with annual attrition at 7.2% in pre-primary, 4.7% in primary and 5.4% in secondary. In 27 of 68 countries analysed, teacher salaries are below those of similarly qualified professionals. The global primary pupil-teacher ratio is about 28 to 1.

title: UNICEF praises India’s progress in girls’ education, says community action is helping curb child...
blurb: At a UN event co-hosted by India and Sierra Leone for the International Day of the Girl Child, UNICEF Deputy Executive Director Hannan Sulieman said India's girls' education has improved significantly over the past decade and child marriage has declined, aided by coordinated government and community efforts. She noted India has 253 million adolescents, so its progress matters globally. India's Permanent Representative Parvathaneni Harish highlighted Beti Bachao Beti Padhao, community engagement and digital public infrastructure, saying investment in girls' education yields compounding returns for families and the economy. Speakers stressed education, health, safety and empowerment as linked priorities.

title: India's school-to-work push faces test of skills, jobs and apprenticeships
blurb: Business Standard reports that the government plans to link education and employment databases and expand career counselling in schools to strengthen the path from school to work. Experts quoted say apprenticeships, training and job creation will be key to improving outcomes.

title: Boys' lower regard for school effort may help explain academic gender gap
blurb: A research summary reported by Phys.org suggests that boys' lower regard for effort at school may help explain the academic gender gap.

title: Under Mission Saksham Anganwadi and Poshan 2.0, various steps have been undertaken to improve the infrastructure facilities at Anganwadi Centres
blurb: The Ministry of Women and Child Development reports that 50,000 Anganwadi Centres are being built during the 15th Finance Commission cycle, at 10,000 a year, with Rs 8 lakh from MGNREGS, Rs 2 lakh from Finance Commission funds and Rs 2 lakh from the Ministry per centre. Funding for drinking water rose from Rs 10,000 to Rs 17,000 and for toilets from Rs 12,000 to Rs 36,000, while two lakh centres are being upgraded as Saksham Anganwadis. Guidelines issued on 3 September 2025 co-locate centres with primary schools to strengthen ECCE and FLN. A new Poshan Tracker Nominee Module lets beneficiaries nominate someone to collect Take-Home Ration.

title: Teacher recruitment – compounding the challenge
blurb: Vikram Sahay argues that NCTE's decision to offer the four-year Integrated Teacher Education Programme (ITEP) in four stage-specific versions, matching NEP 2020's Foundational, Preparatory, Middle and Secondary stages, may complicate teacher recruitment. He notes that recruitment rules and qualifications are currently built around primary, upper primary, secondary and senior secondary levels, with over 18,000 D.El.Ed and B.Ed programmes against about 900 four-year programmes. He says NEP 2020 recommended a four-year integrated B.Ed but did not call for separate courses per stage. Stage-wise qualifications, he argues, could split primary teaching into two qualifications and affect teacher availability, calling for careful alignment.

title: Indore school moves Supreme Court seeking curbs on social media use of children | India News
blurb: Emerald Heights International School in Indore and its director Siddharth Singh have filed a public interest litigation in the Supreme Court seeking an enforceable framework to protect children from social media harms such as cyberbullying, exploitation, harmful content and compulsive use. Citing Articles 14, 15(3), 21 and 21A, the plea asks the court to direct the Union government to frame dedicated rules or set age-based restrictions on children's accounts. Respondents include the Union government, three ministries and the NCPCR, and no hearing date has been set. The plea follows a September 10 order in which a bench led by CJI Surya Kant sought the Centre's response on a related petition.

title: Open minds please: Schools can’t teach children everything but must foster lifelong teaching
blurb: This piece reflects on how earlier scientific consensus, such as claims that only humans make tools or that animals lack morality, was overturned as observers and experimenters gathered new evidence. From this, it argues that schools cannot teach children everything and should instead foster open minds and lifelong learning.

title: CBSE Class 12 special exams for West Asian students from October 23 to 28
blurb: CBSE has issued a timetable, dated October 9, for Class 12 special examinations from October 23 to 28, 2026, for eligible students in Bahrain, Iran, Kuwait, Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the UAE, whose March–April board papers could not be held due to the regional conflict. Exams run on five days, with none on October 25, and most papers from 10.30 am to 1.30 pm. Admit cards are available from October 12, there is one centre per country and no exam fee. Students choose their subjects, and the new marks will replace earlier assessment-scheme results as final, with no post-result facilities.

title: Nandan Nilekani pitches for AI generated question papers, nationwide CBT to avoid paper leaks | Education
blurb: Nandan Nilekani proposed at the Bloomberg New Economy Forum that AI generate exam papers on the day of the test from a large question bank, removing the economic incentive to sell leaked papers. He also called for moving all exams to computer-based testing, saying India's network of 150,000 test locations needs to expand. Nilekani, who heads a committee on these reforms, said the committee would address such systemic issues and that the Prime Minister is keen to implement its decisions. Asked whether AI could create papers on exam day, he answered in the affirmative.

title: Gender and education: What is the latest data and evidence?
blurb: Drawing on UNESCO's 2026 Gender Report, this page finds that global gender parity in enrolment was reached from pre-primary to upper secondary by 2024, while tertiary enrolment now has 88 young men for every 100 young women. Of 273 million out-of-school children and youth in 2024, 140 million were boys and 133 million girls. Gaps persist within countries: in rural India only 59 girls completed upper secondary for every 100 boys, while urban areas had reached parity. Citing progress in Cambodia, Nepal and others, the report recommends combining financial, social and educational measures, including free and compulsory education.

title: New UNESCO data: For every two teachers, the world needs one more
blurb: A UNESCO Institute for Statistics fact sheet for World Teachers' Day 2026 finds that 58% of teachers needed worldwide by 2030 will replace those leaving, with attrition at 7.2% in pre-primary, 5.4% in secondary and 4.7% in primary. In two of five of 68 countries, teacher pay trails similarly qualified professionals, and teachers work about 60 hours a week against 19 in class. In 75% of TALIS 2024 countries, fewer than 40% of teachers felt valued. It recommends involving teachers in policy, career paths, competitive pay, incentives for hard-to-staff schools and less workload, while UNESCO and the ILO revise the 1966 Recommendation through mid-2027.

title: SubscriberWrites: From Degrees to Capabilities: Rethinking India’s Education
blurb: In this reader-contributed piece, the author argues that India should measure education by what young people can do rather than by the degrees they hold. Drawing on NITI Aayog's Reimagining Skilling for Viksit Bharat@2047 report of 18 August 2026, the piece notes that over 7.67 crore people have been formally skilled since 2014-15 and about ₹34,000 crore was allocated for skilling in FY2025-26. It points to a diverse labour force of about 65.4 crore, 58.4% of them self-employed. The author recommends work-integrated degrees, apprenticeships, modular learning and use of the National Credit Framework so vocational learners can move into formal education.

title: DIKSHA: Powering India's Digital Learning Ecosystem
blurb: A Press Information Bureau feature sets out how DIKSHA, launched in 2017 and led by NCERT with CIET, serves as the national digital platform for school education under PM e-Vidya. It offers curriculum-linked K-12 content, from foundational literacy and numeracy to senior secondary, including QR-coded energised textbooks, simulations, more than 614 virtual labs and accessible formats such as DAISY and Indian Sign Language videos. The platform supports 135 languages, 128 of them Indian, works offline, and hosts teacher training through NISHTHA. Its federated design lets states upload content in regional languages, with periodic validation by CIET-NCERT.

title: Coaching as Compensation: What the Red Fort scheme reveals about school education | Hindustan Times
blurb: Avinash Agarwal of Disha Publication argues that the free online coaching network announced from the Red Fort on 15 August 2026 can widen access to competitive-exam preparation by removing cost barriers. Citing the Comprehensive Modular Survey: Education 2025, he notes that 27% of school students have taken private coaching, 30.7% in urban and 25.5% in rural areas. He says the network's value will depend on consistent teaching, relevant content and measurable outcomes, not scale alone. The author recommends strengthening school education so that coaching becomes supplementary, giving students a firm foundation to decide when extra preparation helps.

title: Learning for Tomorrow: How El Salvador Is Using AI to Transform Education
blurb: The World Bank reports that El Salvador is modernising education by combining structured teaching, continuous assessment, teacher training and AI tools aligned with its national curriculum. Before the reform, seven in ten children could not read a simple text by age 10, around 40% of young people did not finish secondary school and one in four youth were neither studying nor working. An AI tutor gives students step-by-step hints while dashboards show teachers where help is needed. Backed by World Bank Program-for-Results financing tied to results, the effort is expected to reach about 500,000 public school students.

title: El Niño Practical Guidance for the Education Sector
blurb: UNICEF and Save the Children have released practical guidance to help education systems prepare for El Niño in 2026–2027. The document notes that climate hazards disrupted schooling for at least 171 million students in 2025, and that over 347 million children in nearly 100 countries and territories live where El Niño may bring unusually wet or dry conditions in late 2026. It pairs system-level recommendations with hazard-specific actions: building climate risk into education planning, identifying the most at-risk schools and learners, strengthening learning continuity plans, and preparing coordination, forecast triggers and financing for anticipatory action, response and recovery.

title: Choosing an international curriculum - What are Indian parents really investing in? | Hindustan Times
blurb: Nitasha Sagar Kukar, founder and CEO of Academio, writes that international curricula are spreading in India, with 274 IB World schools and more than 800 Cambridge schools, nearly half of the latter in Tier 2 and Tier 3 cities. Cambridge's March 2026 series drew over 91,000 entries in India, up 7% year-on-year. She argues that the curriculum is only a framework and that school culture, teachers and daily classroom practice determine its value. She advises parents to look at whether classrooms encourage inquiry, investment in teaching staff, chances for independent thinking, global exposure and student agency.

title: Learning Curve | Latest Issue Out Now!
blurb: The Azim Premji Foundation has announced that a new issue of Learning Curve, its publication on education, is out. The available material does not describe the theme or articles in this issue.

title: Clean India - Clean schools
blurb: UNICEF India's Clean India, Clean Schools page explains how water, sanitation and hygiene facilities support children's health, attendance and learning. It notes that Ministry of Education data show nearly half of schools in India lack basic handwashing facilities, and cites studies finding that a quarter of girls in school took time off during menstruation because of inadequate toilets. It describes the Swachh Bharat, Swachh Vidyalaya initiative launched in 2015 to provide sex-segregated toilets in all government schools. It also outlines the Swachh Vidyalaya Puraskar framework, which UNICEF helped develop, now benchmarking schools on 52 indicators.

title: Listening with Eyes, Reading with Fingers: Redesigning Foundational Numeracy Assessment to Include the Children Most Left Behind
blurb: PAL Network describes how it is redesigning its International Common Assessment of Numeracy (ICAN) so children with visual and hearing impairments can be included in foundational learning measurement. Using Universal Design for Learning, it changes how questions are delivered and answered, for example real objects in place of printed charts, tactile cards and Braille instructions, without changing the skills measured. Sightsavers provides technical guidance, ITA leads testing in Pakistan and The Action Foundation adapts the tool in Kenya, including Kenyan Sign Language, with education ministries involved. Washington Group questions on child functioning allow results to be broken down by disability type.

title: Only 59 Rural Indian Girls Complete Higher Secondary Education For Every 100 Boys: UNESCO
blurb: According to a UNESCO report, only 59 girls in rural India complete higher secondary education for every 100 boys. The gender parity index for upper-secondary completion is 0.59 in rural areas, 1.00 in urban areas and 0.89 nationally.

title: AI in the classroom needs teachers in the driver’s seat, global study finds
blurb: A Cambridge research paper based on interviews with 15 English language teachers and trainers in 13 countries finds that generative AI helps with lesson planning, adapting materials to different levels, quizzes and feedback, but works best when teachers stay in charge. Teachers reported concerns about accuracy, bias, privacy and students turning to AI before trying tasks themselves, which could weaken independent thinking. The report argues that AI literacy should include knowing when not to use AI and how to judge its output. It recommends policies rooted in classroom practice, sustained professional development and rethinking assessment.

title: Literacy for All
blurb: A Press Information Bureau note traces India's literacy progress, from 18.32% in 1951 to 74.04% in 2011, and an overall rate of 81.1% according to PLFS 2025. The Ministry of Education now defines literacy to include comprehension and life skills such as digital and financial literacy, treating 95% as full literacy. The note cites UDISE+ 2025-26 figures of over 24.72 crore students enrolled, 91.7% GER at the preparatory stage and 7.0% secondary dropout, and higher education enrolment rising from 3.42 crore to 4.50 crore. It highlights ULLAS and NIPUN Bharat as key initiatives under NEP 2020.

title: NCERT Announces Online Diploma Course In Science Teaching: Registration From October 12
blurb: NCERT has announced an online diploma course in science teaching, with registration opening on 12 October. The available material does not give details on eligibility, duration or course content.

title: Education ministry holds nationwide screening on inclusive education for children with special needs
blurb: The Ministry of Education held a nationwide screening of a 30-minute orientation module on inclusive education for children with special needs through the PRASHAST portal. Available in 12 Indian languages, the module is meant for school heads, teachers, special educators and non-teaching staff such as drivers, clerks and wardens, supporting a whole-school approach to inclusion. The ministry said over 72 lakh teachers have already been sensitised and 60,000 schools took part, with participation expected to grow this month. PRASHAST uses a two-part teacher checklist to screen for probable disabilities under the RPwD Act, 2016, with special educators validating cases and arranging referrals.

title: They still call us ‘jungli’. For Adivasi kids, free school comes at a cost
blurb: This Times of India report looks at the experiences of Adivasi children in school, including being called 'jungli', and the costs that families can face even when schooling is free.

title: From India to France: Why are Gen Z students angry?
blurb: The article compares the School Thik Karo campaign, launched on 15 August by the Cockroach Janata Party to audit basic facilities in government schools, with student protests that began in Créteil, France, in September. The Indian campaign uses volunteers, parents and students to check sanitation, drinking water, electricity and building safety, passing findings to gram panchayats and school committees. In France, protests over crowded classrooms, teacher shortages and spending cuts affected over 1,000 high schools by 1 October, with around 2.5 lakh demonstrators by government estimates, and have spread to several European countries. The piece notes France's tight finances, with education spending at 6.7% of GDP.

title: AI-powered scams raise stakes of student data breaches, cybersecurity expert warns
blurb: Cybersecurity expert Sarthak Dubey warns that EdTech platforms can expose student data through the third-party services they use, such as payment gateways, cloud providers and messaging tools. Drawing on running a platform holding data on over 600,000 students, he says leaked details could be combined with AI voice cloning to create convincing scams aimed at parents. He lists common weaknesses including shared admin passwords, missing multi-factor authentication and lingering vendor access, and notes the DPDP Act, 2023 includes safeguards for children's data. He recommends mapping data flows, vetting vendors, collecting minimal data, continuous monitoring, tested incident-response plans and clear guidance for parents.

title: The environment is flooded with information and problems for French students.
blurb: PISA 2025 results show average performance across OECD countries at its lowest since the assessment began, with scores falling 22 points in maths and 28 points in reading between 2015 and 2025. The share of 15-year-olds performing poorly in all three areas rose to 20% from 16% in 2022. France scored 483 in science, near the OECD average, but has lost 18 points in reading and 16 in maths since 2022. Drawing on a French planning commission report, the analysis argues that trends matter more than rankings and points to modest primary spending, high pupil-teacher ratios and teacher recruitment difficulties.

title: Teacher Pay Across Europe: OECD 2026 Salary Data and Labor Protests - News and Statistics
blurb: OECD Education at a Glance 2026 data covering 28 education systems show that actual salaries for primary school teachers in 2025 ranged from EUR18,669 in Turkey to EUR74,086 in Denmark. Iceland, Ireland, Germany and Austria follow Denmark, all above EUR65,000, while France stands at EUR41,968 and Italy at EUR32,100. Seven countries report salaries below EUR25,000, including Czechia, Hungary, Slovakia, Romania, Latvia, Greece and Turkey. The coverage notes that teachers generally earn less than similarly educated workers and that French unions are pressing for higher pay and better staffing.

title: Union education minister urges students to focus on innovation to build developed India
blurb: Speaking in Patna at a felicitation for the Seva Sankalp Abhiyan painting and speech competitions, which drew students from 95,195 schools across 38 Bihar districts, Union Minister Prahlad Joshi urged students to focus on innovation to help build a developed India by 2047. He said NEP 2020 promotes critical thinking and creativity beyond exams and jobs, and asked parents and teachers to respect children's interests. He cited PM SHRI schools and Atal Tinkering Labs, textbooks in 22 Indian languages and DIKSHA content in 128 Indian languages. He also said Rs 1 lakh crore has been earmarked in the Union budget for innovation.

title: Education Ministry conducts nationwide screening on inclusive education through PRASHAST portal
blurb: The Department of School Education and Literacy held a nationwide screening on 8 October of a 30-minute orientation module on inclusive education for children with special needs through the PRASHAST portal. More than 60,000 schools took part, and over 72 lakh teachers had been sensitised through the module in the previous three months. Offered in 12 Indian languages, the module targets school heads, teachers, special educators and non-teaching staff. PRASHAST helps teachers screen for probable disabilities under the RPwD Act, 2016, with special educators validating cases and arranging referrals; it supports early identification but does not provide medical diagnosis.

title: NCERT to Host 4-Day Online Training Programme On Effective Communication For Educators
blurb: NCERT is hosting a four-day online training programme for educators on effective communication. The available material does not give dates, registration details or session topics.

title: Births of girls rise in India: 15 more girls per 1,000 children, but rural girls lag in completing education
blurb: Research on the initial districts covered by the Beti Bachao, Beti Padhao campaign estimates that it led to around 15 additional girls per 1,000 births, with the strongest effect in families whose first child was a daughter, where 37 to 53 additional girls per 1,000 births are estimated. India's sex ratio at birth has risen from 919 girls per 1,000 boys in 2015-16 to 930. Separately, a UNESCO report on gender equality in access to education across 31 low- and middle-income countries finds that 89 girls complete upper secondary education in India for every 100 boys. In rural areas, only 59 girls per 100 boys complete Classes 11 and 12.

title: Rethinking the purpose of education systems transformation
blurb: Brookings has published a study from the Network for Education Systems Transformation (NEST), produced with partners Dream a Dream in India, Enseña Perú and SmartStart in South Africa, on rethinking the purpose of education systems transformation.

title: PISA 2025 shows declining reading scores across much of Europe, with Latvia among hardest hit
blurb: PISA 2025 recorded the lowest OECD-average reading performance yet, down 28 points since 2015, with significant declines since 2018 in 56 of 74 systems. Across Central, Eastern and Southern Europe, Latvia fell most, by 45 points to 430, after moving to Latvian as the sole language of instruction, while Slovenia dropped 24 points to 445, its lowest since 2006. Estonia led the region with 499 and Poland scored 482, both above the OECD average of 461; Ukraine's 418 showed no significant change despite the war. Slovenia's minister announced reforms covering curricula, assessment, earlier literacy teaching and support for struggling students.

title: Is girls’ education a problem of the past?
blurb: A post on UNESCO's World Education Blog asks whether girls' education can now be considered a problem of the past.

title: Lessons Under Air-Raid Sirens: An Analysis of PISA 2025 Result
blurb: An analysis of Ukraine's PISA 2025 results finds students scoring 448 in science, 431 in mathematics and 418 in reading, below OECD averages of 486, 469 and 466. Scores are slightly lower than in 2022 and well below 2018, with the largest fall between 2018 and 2022, a pattern seen across many OECD countries. Girls lead boys by 32 points in reading, and students in small settlements score lowest. Overall, 56.4% of students did not reach baseline proficiency in at least one domain.

title: Global consultations on education in the age of AI
blurb: A new discussion paper, Sustaining education as a common good in the age of AI: The case for deliberative governance, identifies six directional shifts through which education's public purposes are undermined when AI use is ungoverned. It anchors a series of background papers on topics including AI procurement, total cost of ownership, learner safety, explainable AI, age-appropriateness and digital sovereignty. A global consultation runs from September to November 2026 for experts, academics and officials, and the feedback will shape a compilation of policy briefs to be released during Digital Learning Week 2027.

title: Why are 51% of India's five-year-olds already in primary school? UNESCO report raises concerns
blurb: UNESCO's 2026 Global Education Monitoring Report finds that 51% of India's five-year-olds are enrolled in primary school rather than pre-primary education, against 27% of children one year below entry age worldwide. UDISE+ data show this share rose from about 35% in 2019 and 2020 to 60% in 2022, while the proportion of Class 1 entrants with preschool experience grew from 41% in 2019 to 80% in 2025. The report notes that early childhood education is shared between Anganwadis and state pre-primary classes, and cites Indian evidence that preschool fee scholarships raised participation by 20 percentage points. NEP 2020 recommends Class 1 entry at age six.

title: India’s rural gender gap in upper-secondary completion remains stark despite wider progress: UNESCO report | India News
blurb: A UNESCO Global Education Monitoring report, 'Gender Equity in Access to Education', finds India has an adjusted gender parity index of 0.89 for upper-secondary completion, falling to 0.59 in rural areas, where 59 girls finish for every 100 boys, while urban areas have reached parity. It cites Indian evidence that free school lunches raised girls' primary enrolment nearly twice as much as boys', and that latrine construction increased enrolment among pubescent girls. Across Central and Southern Asia, girls' upper-secondary completion rose from 12% in 2000 to 57% in 2024. The report calls for coordinated measures on affordability, meals, proximity, sanitation, safety and second-chance pathways.

title: 51% of India’s 5-year-olds in Class 1 instead of preschool: UNESCO report flags concern | India News
blurb: UNESCO's 2026 Global Education Monitoring report finds that 51% of India's five-year-olds are enrolled in primary school rather than pre-primary education, citing UDISE+ data showing the share of under-six children in primary rose from about 35% in 2019-20 to 60% in 2022. It cautions that the share entering Class 1 with preschool experience grew from 41% in 2019 to 80% in 2025. The report notes provision is split between Anganwadi centres and state pre-primary classes. NEP 2020 recommends Class 1 entry at age six, and the ministry asked states in February 2023 to align admission age, supported by Bal Vatika and Vidya Pravesh.

title: Gender gaps in education narrow globally, yet early marriage remains a
blurb: UNESCO's 2026 Global Education Monitoring Gender Report, issued for the International Day of the Girl Child, finds that girls and boys now enrol in equal numbers from pre-primary to upper secondary, with Nepal closing a 33-point gap in lower secondary completion and Cambodia moving girls from 22 points behind to 11 ahead in primary completion. Gaps persist among rural and poor households; in rural India, 59 girls complete upper secondary for every 100 boys. Child marriage fell from 25% in 2000 to 18% in 2025. The report urges practical support such as transport, childcare and sanitation, alongside legal protection for pregnant and parenting girls.

title: Department of School Education & Literacy, Ministry of Education, Organises Nationwide Screening of Inclusive Education Sensitization Module through PRASHAST
blurb: The Department of School Education and Literacy in the Ministry of Education has organised a nationwide screening of its Inclusive Education Sensitization Module through PRASHAST. The screening takes the module to audiences across the country as part of the Department's work on inclusive education. It is intended to build sensitivity and awareness around the inclusion of children with diverse needs in schools.

title: AI in the classroom: Are students in India ready for a machine-run world?
blurb: The Week's piece considers whether students in India are prepared for a world increasingly run by artificial intelligence, and what AI's growing presence in classrooms means for them.

title: 2 Education Startups Help Raise The Bar As Students’ Math Scores Plummet In India
blurb: NCERT's PARAKH Rashtriya Sarvekshan 2024 found that average maths scores drop from 60 per cent in Class 3 to 37 per cent in Class 9, a decline educators link to rote memorisation. At India Mobile Congress 2026, two startups showcased activity-based tools in response. EduMEasy, founded by IITians, has set up maths labs in over 500 schools, with NCERT-aligned workbooks, bilingual teacher manuals and an app for Classes 1 to 10. Wooda presented patented hands-on learning kits aligned with NCF 2023, including a Braille-integrated design so that visually impaired children can learn alongside classmates.

title: United Nations Body Shares Framework To Make Teachers AI-Ready
blurb: A United Nations body has released a framework intended to help teachers become ready to use artificial intelligence.

title: How state policymakers can address unequal access to adequate school facilities
blurb: This Brookings piece, by researchers including Lucy Sorensen of the Learning Policy Institute, looks at how state policymakers in the United States can tackle unequal access to adequate school facilities. It notes that local property wealth drives racial gaps in facility quality and sets out policy options for states.

title: TIE-EdLab: driving evidence-informed education in Tanzania
source: What Works Hub for Global Education
blurb: This blog describes the Tanzania Institute of Education Laboratory (TIE-EdLab), set up in December 2023 with Georgetown University, the University of Dar es Salaam and the University of Delaware as a government-embedded research unit producing actionable evidence on learning. Because TIE designs the national curriculum and teaching materials, research can feed directly into policy. An Advisory Board co-chaired by the education ministry and PMO-RALG sets the agenda and meets every February. The authors say evidence uptake depends on trust, timing and relationships as well as data quality, and is supported by Friday sessions, policy briefs and training for officials.

title: PISA 2025: Reading proficiency can be developed--even among older adolescents and adults
blurb: A press release headlined on PISA 2025 states that reading proficiency can be developed even among older adolescents and adults.

title: Why schools must teach children to be active citizens
blurb: In this piece, Aruna Sankaranarayanan, visiting faculty at Azim Premji University, argues that schools should teach children to become active citizens.

title: Key data on girls and women’s right to education
blurb: UNESCO's HerAtlas tracks 12 legal indicators on girls' and women's right to education and finds that national laws have grown more comprehensive since 2019: 64 countries now reach the top score on at least six indicators, compared with 49 in 2019. Progress is clearest in raising the minimum marriage age, protecting against violence in schools and safeguarding pregnant and parenting girls' education. Yet nearly half of countries still lack explicit protection for pregnant and parenting girls or allow marriage below 18. UNESCO says education laws need to work together with laws on marriage, work and violence.

title: Mission Guidance Note for Foundational Learning Engagements (English)
blurb: The World Bank has issued a Mission Guidance Note for Foundational Learning Engagements, available in English and Spanish. It guides technical missions that help task teams analyse education systems, shape project design and support supervision.

title: School Meals in Crisis Settings: Costs, Trade-offs, and Delivery Choices in Education-in-Emergencies Programmes
blurb: The Center for Global Development examines school meals in crisis settings, looking at their costs, trade-offs and delivery choices within education-in-emergencies programmes.

title: The hidden crisis in Indian classrooms: Why teachers are quitting before year five
blurb: Writing for World Teachers' Day, Latika Gupta draws on UNESCO's 2023 Global Report on Teachers, which found that many teachers leave within five years, especially at the primary level, and cited a shortage of 7.8 million teachers in South Asia. The author argues that motivation and preparation are central: she notes that primary teaching experience does not count towards becoming a principal, limiting career progression. She points to Delhi University's four-year B.El.Ed. Programme as an example whose graduates showed lasting commitment, and calls for teacher education rather than narrow skills training.

title: Report of the Regional Workshop on Inclusive Education (CwSN) and Nasha Mukt Vidyalaya for North-East
blurb: The Department of School Education and Literacy in the Ministry of Education has released the report of a regional workshop for the North-East. The workshop covered two areas: inclusive education for children with special needs (CwSN) and Nasha Mukt Vidyalaya, the effort to keep schools drug-free. The report documents the regional deliberations on both themes as part of the Ministry's ongoing work with the North-Eastern states on inclusion and student wellbeing.

title: NCERT Diploma Course 2026: Registration opens October 12 at ncert.nic.in, here's how to apply
blurb: NCERT has announced an online diploma course on Teaching of Science at the Middle Stage, aimed at teachers of Classes 6 to 8. Registration opens on October 12, 2026 and closes on November 12 through ncert.nic.in, with the course running from November 16, 2026 to August 31, 2027. Science teachers, B.Sc graduates, education diploma or degree holders and pre-service teachers across India are eligible. The programme has 40 interactive, multimedia modules of about 6 to 8 hours each, released weekly on Mondays, followed by a final examination.

title: Implementation Science for Scaling in Education
blurb: The World Bank and the What Works Hub for Global Education run the Implementation Science for Scaling in Education programme, launched in 2024 under the Foundational Learning Compact, to help governments deliver proven approaches at scale. It measures gaps in classroom delivery, explains their causes and closes them through iterative adaptation, and has worked in 9 countries as of October 2026. In Cambodia, a survey on structured pedagogy found weaknesses in training, mentoring and book access; an A/B test across three provinces is now running. The work could reach 40,300 grade 1-3 teachers and 1.7 million students.

title: NCERT announces online diploma in science teaching for Classes 6 to 8
blurb: NCERT has launched a 40-week online diploma, "Teaching of Science at Middle Stage", for Classes 6 to 8, offered on the NCERTX platform. Registration for the 2026-27 batch runs from October 12 to November 12, 2026, and the course runs from November 16 to around August 31, 2027. It has 40 weekly modules needing six to eight hours a week, with a one-time fee of Rs 2,000. BSc graduates, in-service and pre-service teachers and others in science education may enrol. NCERT clarifies it is a professional-development programme and not a teacher-recruitment qualification.

title: World needs 50 million additional teachers by 2030, UNESCO says
blurb: New UNESCO data released on World Teachers' Day project that the world will need 50 million more teachers by 2030: 44 million for universal primary and secondary education and 6 million for pre-primary. The joint message from UNESCO, the ILO, UNICEF and Education International, marking 60 years of the Recommendation concerning the Status of Teachers, calls for professional recognition and fair pay. Pre-primary and primary teachers earn slightly less than similarly qualified professionals, and in 75% of TALIS 2024 countries fewer than 40% of teachers felt valued. Up to 273 million children are out of school.

title: 50 million teachers needed by 2030, mostly to replace those leaving
blurb: UNESCO's summary for World Teachers' Day, published on October 5, estimates that 50 million teachers must be recruited by 2030, with 58% of that need arising from replacing teachers who leave. The total includes 44 million for primary and secondary and 6 million for pre-primary education, against a current workforce of 107 million. Sub-Saharan Africa alone needs 15 million primary and secondary teachers by 2030. In two out of five of the 68 countries examined, teachers earn less than comparably qualified professionals, and UNESCO recommends better pay, career progression and working conditions.

title: NCERT opens registration for 40-week Science teaching diploma for Classes 6-8
blurb: NCERT has opened registration for a 40-week online Diploma in Teaching of Science at Middle Stage for 2026-27, aimed at in-service and pre-service teachers handling Classes 6 to 8. The MOOC on the NCERTX platform releases one module every Monday from 16 November 2026, each with an objective test, and ends with a final examination and an e-certificate. Applications are open until 12 November, with a one-time fee of Rs 2,000. NCERT clarifies that it is an academic course and not a recruitment qualification.

title: PISA tests: Students in the EU are increasingly lagging behind others in advanced countries
blurb: Recent PISA results show students in the European Union increasingly falling behind their peers in other advanced countries.

title: Teachers for All: Advancing Equity-based Teacher Deployment in Sierra Leone
blurb: This UNICEF report, prepared with Sierra Leone's Ministry of Basic and Senior Secondary Education and the Teaching Service Commission, uses 2022 School Census and Primary Examination data to map teacher shortages and deployment. It finds weak foundational learning is linked to under-qualified teachers, uneven allocation across provinces and remote areas, and overcrowded early-grade classrooms. It recommends using data to send newly qualified teachers where need is greatest, bringing qualified volunteer teachers onto the payroll where feasible, offering incentives for remote postings and strengthening teaching through coaching and Teaching at the Right Level.

title: Local evidence changes policy: Research highlights how Senegal accomplished groundbreaking bilingual education reform
blurb: A study in the International Journal of Bilingual Education and Bilingualism examines how Senegal moved toward bilingual schooling after years of teaching only in French, although fewer than 1 percent of adults speak it as a first language. Earlier national attempts in 1977-84 and 2002-08 faced limited teaching materials, trained teachers and parental support. A 2008-19 pilot across nine school districts, reaching over 10,000 students, showed that learning in a home language improved reading and maths and helped French skills too. The authors conclude that locally generated evidence gave policymakers the confidence to scale the reform.

title: Are we asking teachers to do more without preparing them to succeed?
blurb: This World Education Blog post asks whether teachers are being given enough preparation to succeed as expectations of them grow.

title: Teachers navigating transformations driven by AI, climate change, migration: UNESCO report
blurb: A UNESCO report for World Teachers' Day says the world needs 50 million additional teachers by 2030 to achieve universal pre-primary to secondary education, with 58 per cent of demand arising from replacing those who leave. Annual attrition stands at 7.2 per cent in pre-primary, 4.7 per cent in primary and 5.4 per cent in secondary education, and salaries trail similarly qualified professionals in 27 of 68 countries. Fewer than 40 per cent of teachers feel valued by society. The report urges stronger recognition and support, and notes a ministerial statement that AI should support, not replace, teachers.

title: EU faces uphill struggle as one in three teens underachieves in school
blurb: The Brussels Times reports that about one in three teenagers in the EU is underachieving in school, leaving the bloc with a difficult task in raising basic skills.

title: Problem with school History books isn’t just the facts. It’s what they aren’t teaching
blurb: In this opinion piece, historian Manu V Devadevan discusses NCERT's new Class 9 Social Science textbook, Understanding Society: India and Beyond - Part 2. The author argues that recent History textbook revisions place more weight on chronological events and selected periods than on historical processes that build critical thinking. He says the chapter on the independence movement does not discuss colonialism and nationalism conceptually or cover constitutional reforms, and questions how a chapter on the 13th to 17th centuries frames religious and cultural change. He makes the case for textbooks that encourage enquiry into how societies changed over time.

title: NMMSS Scholarship Application Deadline Extended to October 31, 2026
blurb: The Ministry of Education's Department of School Education and Literacy has extended the application deadline for the NMMSS scholarship to October 31, 2026. Eligible students who have not yet applied now have until that date to submit their applications for the scholarship.

title: National Council's New Class 9 Social Science Textbook Teaches Students How To Start A Business
blurb: NCERT's new Class 9 Social Science textbook includes material that teaches students how to start a business.

title: Kiribati Teachers Prepare Students For Digital Future Amid Limited Connectivity: UNESCO Report
blurb: As reported by NDTV, a UNESCO report describes how teachers in Kiribati are preparing students for a digital future despite limited internet connectivity.

title: From Readiness to Real Change: What Ghana and Malawi Teach Us About Digital Inclusion for Learners with Neurodevelopmental Disabilities
blurb: Drawing on EdTech Hub research in Ghana and a 2026 baseline evaluation in six primary schools in Malawi's Lilongwe and Salima districts, this blog finds that digital tools can help learners with neurodevelopmental disabilities, but only within a wider support system. In Ghana, digital screening, individualised education plans and remote supervision showed promise and improved communication, though device access, connectivity and teachers' digital skills were limited. In Malawi, schools were ready and committed, but capacity was the main constraint, with severe shortages of trained special needs teachers. The authors stress infrastructure, skills and education-health coordination.

title: Lessons on Tech-Enabled Inclusive Education in Ghana: Nudges and Real Behavioural Change
blurb: EdTech Hub draws lessons from two Ghana studies. An 18-month SMS nudge study across 7 Northern Ghana districts, reaching 4,756 caregivers and 546 teachers, found that extra tailored or community-focused messages did not significantly raise attendance compared with baseline reminders; poverty, child labour and literacy barriers limited impact, though messages with school calendar dates helped. A 2025-26 project with Ghana's Special Education Division in 13 Greater Accra schools screened 321 of 389 learners for autism, identifying 38 (11.8%) needing follow-up. The authors conclude that technology must address structural realities and connect with community support.
